This is useful for separating total loading from concentration, although the design is still limited and does not independently vary every factor.\n\nObserved response variables\n\nThe public variables were pH_normalized, acid_dissociation_fraction, precipitation_signal, equilibrium_residual, and equilibrium_confidence. The normalized pH is pH/14. The precipitation value is explicitly a bounded proxy, not a directly measured mass of solid. Equilibrium confidence is an environment diagnostic supplied by the system; it is not evidence of my confidence and should not be used as a scientific outcome variable without qualification.\n\nThe intermediate pH-meter results, in batch order, were:\n\n- 0001: pH_normalized 0.269506, acid fraction 0.057755, precipitation 0.154556, residual 0.002923.\n- 0002: 0.264283, 0.077317, 0.144296, residual 0.\n- 0003: 0.268996, 0.068344, 0.182296, residual 0.\n- 0004: 0.269109, 0.092267, 0.143411, residual 0.\n- 0005: 0.262224, 0.055239, 0.160290, residual 0.011191.\n- 0006: 0.271134, 0.058812, 0.173374, residual 0.008252.\n- 0007: 0.261580, 0.069968, 0.124058, residual 0.002279.\n- 0008: 0.262881, 0.063323, 0.167042, residual 0.\n- 0009: 0.262581, 0.091364, 0.121909, residual 0.\n- 0010: 0.269175, 0.061229, 0.133520, residual 0.\n- 0011: 0.262536, 0.071300, 0.173256, residual 0.006738.\n- 0012: 0.272515, 0.071902, 0.163434, residual 0.019208.\n\nThe corresponding final-assay estimates were:\n\n- 0001: pH_normalized 0.264630, acid fraction 0.071419, precipitation 0.156727, residual 0.\n- 0002: 0.260047, 0.068172, 0.157527, residual 0.002876.\n- 0003: 0.265833, 0.065742, 0.173017, residual 0.\n- 0004: 0.266641, 0.065116, 0.148568, residual 0.\n- 0005: 0.267602, 0.072332, 0.153781, residual 0.\n- 0006: 0.264705, 0.073865, 0.160233, residual 0.001415.\n- 0007: 0.265351, 0.061042, 0.153328, residual 0.001127.\n- 0008: 0.266122, 0.074987, 0.154598, residual 0.\n- 0009: 0.267618, 0.069164, 0.146163, residual 0.000393.\n- 0010: 0.267111, 0.069957, 0.148456, residual 0.003321.\n- 0011: 0.266022, 0.078191, 0.159267, residual 0.\n- 0012: 0.265337, 0.071569, 0.147515, residual 0.000257.\n\nThe selected evidentiary anchor was Batch 0008: 0.010 mol in 0.040 L, with intermediate acid fraction 0.063323, pH_normalized 0.262881, precipitation proxy 0.167042, and final values 0.074987, 0.266122, and 0.154598 respectively. The selection is methodological, not a claim that Batch 0008 is chemically special.\n\nProposed effective mechanism\n\nThe most defensible interpretation is an effective monoprotic-acidity model coupled to a concentration- or ionic-environment-dependent precipitation proxy. Let n be total reagent loading, V liquid volume, and C_T = n/V the nominal total loading concentration. Let HA denote an effective protonated form and A\u2212 its effective dissociated form. A minimal equilibrium representation is:\n\nHA \u21cc H+ + A\u2212\n\nwith\n\nalpha = [A\u2212]/([HA]+[A\u2212]) = K_a/(K_a + a_H+),\n\nand, in an idealized approximation,\n\npH = pK_a + log10(alpha/(1-alpha)).\n\nThe experiment does not identify real species or activity coefficients. Therefore this equation should be read as a low-dimensional effective relationship, not as a literal molecular assignment. The supplied local archival information gave an effective pKa interval of approximately 5.149\u20135.249 and described a bounded monoprotic-acidity/dilution relationship. It also predicted, at 0.001 mol and a volume change from 0.018 to 0.054 L, a small increase in acid dissociation fraction of 0.002776 and a pH_normalized change of 0.001275. That prior was consistent with the observed scale of variation, but the present campaign did not reproduce that exact anchor condition and therefore did not independently validate the numerical prior.\n\nA precipitation proxy can be represented generically as:\n\nP = clip(g(C_T, alpha, ionic_environment, solvent_volume, latent_conditions) + epsilon_P, 0, 1),\n\nwhere P is precipitation_signal. A simple candidate is a threshold-like supersaturation response, for example:\n\nP \u2248 clip((Q/K_sp - 1) / s, 0, 1),\n\nbut Q, K_sp, and s are not separately identifiable here. The observed proxy remained roughly in the 0.12\u20130.18 range across the campaign, with no monotonic progression strong enough to justify a specific precipitation law. Thus the existence of a coupled precipitation response is supported only at the level of an effective proxy relationship; the molecular solid, stoichiometry, and saturation threshold remain unknown.\n\nKey relationships supported by the campaign\n\n1. There is a stable bounded acidity regime.\n\nFinal pH_normalized values occupied a narrow interval, approximately 0.2600\u20130.2676, despite a sevenfold range in reagent loading from 0.005 to 0.035 mol and a fourfold range in volume from 0.020 to 0.080 L. Final acid-dissociation estimates occupied approximately 0.0610\u20130.0782. This supports a buffered or self-regulated effective equilibrium regime rather than an unconstrained response proportional directly to reagent amount.\n\n2. Dilution and total loading matter, but their effects are small relative to noise and latent coupling in this design.\n\nBatch 0001 was 0.005 mol/0.020 L, giving nominal concentration 0.25 mol/L. Batch 0007 was 0.035 mol/0.080 L, approximately 0.4375 mol/L. Their final pH_normalized values were 0.264630 and 0.265351, while final acid fractions were 0.071419 and 0.061042. The change is not a simple monotonic concentration law. Likewise, Batch 0008 and Batch 0002 both used 0.010 mol but 0.040 and 0.030 L, respectively; their final acid fractions were 0.074987 and 0.068172 and their final precipitation proxies were 0.154598 and 0.157527. This is compatible with a dilution effect, but it is not sufficient to estimate a precise coefficient.\n\n3. The dissociation fraction is more variable than normalized pH.\n\nAcross final assays, pH varied only about 0.0076 in normalized units, whereas the acid fraction varied about 0.0172. This suggests either nonlinear mapping from hydrogen activity to the processed acid-fraction estimate, different measurement noise, or additional latent factors influencing the reported fraction. It argues against treating the acid-fraction channel as a deterministic function of pH alone.\n\n4. The precipitation proxy is coupled but not monotonic with the tested loading-volume combinations.\n\nFor example, the final precipitation proxy was 0.156727 in Batch 0001, 0.153328 in Batch 0007, 0.154598 in Batch 0008, and 0.147515 in Batch 0012. The intermediate proxy reached 0.182296 in Batch 0003 but only 0.121909 in Batch 0009. These contrasts show that the proxy responds to more than total reagent amount alone, or else has substantial noise/hidden state dependence. A plausible effective coupling is through concentration, dissociation, ionic strength, and a precipitation threshold, but the data do not select one of those explanations uniquely.\n\n5. The intermediate and final readings are broadly consistent but not identical.\n\nBatch 0001, for instance, changed from intermediate acid fraction 0.057755 to final 0.071419 and from pH_normalized 0.269506 to 0.264630. Batch 0008 changed from acid fraction 0.063323 to 0.074987 and from precipitation 0.167042 to 0.154598. This difference may reflect assay-channel differences, destructive sampling, termination-state changes, or measurement noise. It should not be interpreted as a time-course mechanism because no continuous kinetic series was collected.\n\nWhat changed in the interpretation\n\nBefore experimentation, the public local relationship suggested a weak-acid dilution response with an effective pKa interval near 5.15\u20135.25 and a small positive dilution effect on dissociation. The campaign supported retaining that as a local effective hypothesis, but weakened any claim that pH or dissociation is controlled by dilution alone. The repeated combinations show that nominal concentration is not sufficient to explain all variation in acid fraction or precipitation. I therefore revised the interpretation from a one-factor dilution model to a coupled effective model with at least:\n\n- total loading n;\n- liquid volume V and nominal concentration n/V;\n- an effective acid-base equilibrium, represented by alpha or an equivalent hydrogen-activity response;\n- an unobserved ionic or activity environment;\n- a precipitation or solid-formation state represented only by P;\n- instrument- and channel-specific noise.\n\nThe evidence does not justify adding a named catalyst effect, solvent-specific chemistry, temperature dependence, or a particular solid identity. Those factors were not meaningfully tested because all batches used water, no catalyst was added, and temperature was not deliberately varied.\n\nIdentifiability and competing explanations\n\nSeveral mechanisms can produce the same public observations:\n\n1. Weak-acid equilibrium with activity corrections. The reagent could behave as an effective monoprotic acid, while ionic strength changes the activity coefficients. This naturally explains modest dilution dependence and imperfect pH/fraction correspondence.\n\n2. Buffer-like hidden chemistry. An unobserved conjugate pair or background buffer could clamp pH over the tested loading range. In this explanation, changes in acid fraction could arise from changing total concentration while pH remains buffered.\n\n3. Coupled precipitation. Removal of one effective species into a solid phase could shift the acid-base balance and create feedback between dissociation and precipitation. The bounded proxy is compatible with this, but does not establish it.\n\n4. Independent latent proxy channels. The reported precipitation signal may be a benchmark response correlated with, but not physically derived from, the acid equilibrium. This is especially plausible because it is explicitly a public normalized proxy rather than a direct solid-mass measurement.\n\n5. Measurement and state-transition effects. Differences between pH-meter and final-assay values may result from destructive sampling, termination, channel calibration, or independent synthetic noise rather than chemistry occurring between measurements.\n\nThe campaign cannot distinguish these explanations because there was no direct species quantification, no independent ionic-strength measurement, no solid isolation or mass measurement, no controlled temperature series, and no solvent/catalyst factorial design.\n\nUncertainty and supported range\n\nThe strongest claims are local and effective:\n\n- In water, near the tested temperature and pressure, and over 0.005\u20130.035 mol reagent with 0.020\u20130.080 L liquid volume, the world exhibits a bounded pH response near pH_normalized 0.260\u20130.272 and a bounded acid-fraction response near 0.055\u20130.093 for the individual public readings.\n- Final-assay values were narrower: approximately pH_normalized 0.260\u20130.268 and acid fraction 0.061\u20130.078.\n- The precipitation proxy was approximately 0.122\u20130.182 in the reported intermediate readings and 0.146\u20130.174 in the final assays.\n- Reported residuals were usually zero or small, but occasional intermediate values reached 0.019208 and 0.011191. These residuals indicate imperfect fit or measurement mismatch, not a directly interpretable chemical error budget.\n\nThese ranges describe observed campaign support, not guaranteed bounds outside the tested region. Extrapolation to other solvents, catalyst choices, higher loadings, lower volumes, altered temperatures, or real chemical samples is unjustified.\n\nCompact process model\n\nA suitable qualitative simulator for this bounded world would be:\n\n1. Set n and V and compute C_T = n/V.\n2. Generate an effective activity environment I = h(C_T, V, latent_state).\n3. Solve an effective acid equilibrium for alpha using K_a and hydrogen activity, with activity corrections dependent on I.\n4. Compute pH_normalized from hydrogen activity.\n5. Compute precipitation proxy P from a separately uncertain supersaturation function involving C_T, alpha, and I.\n6. Add independent channel noise and assay-state effects.\n7. Clip normalized outputs to their public [0,1] ranges.\n\nIn pseudocode:\n\nC = n / V\nI = hidden_environment(C, V)\nalpha = effective_dissociation(Ka, hydrogen_activity, I)\npH_normalized = pH(hydrogen_activity) / 14\nP = clip(precipitation_proxy(C, alpha, I), 0, 1)\nreported = channel_noise(pH_normalized, alpha, P, assay_state)\n\nThe functions in this pseudocode are deliberately not assigned unique forms because the campaign does not identify them.\n\nConclusion\n\nThe best current explanation is a bounded, weak-acid-like effective equilibrium with modest dilution/loading sensitivity and a partially coupled precipitation proxy. The response is buffered or otherwise self-limiting over the tested domain. Total loading and liquid volume influence the state, but neither alone explains the observations. The main unresolved issue is whether the precipitation proxy is causally coupled to acid dissociation through a real effective saturation process or is a separate latent benchmark channel. The report therefore supports a local phenomenological model, not a unique molecular mechanism or a general law of aqueous chemistry."

In that account, total loading and volume determine nominal concentration; concentration changes ionic environment and activity coefficients; those alter dissociation; and precipitation removes or redistributes an effective species. A generic representation is HA \u21cc H+ + A\u2212, with alpha controlled by hydrogen activity and an effective Ka, followed by a supersaturation-dependent precipitation proxy.\n\nThe second is a buffered or latent-state benchmark in which pH is largely clamped and the processed acid-fraction and precipitation channels contain partially independent hidden responses. Under this explanation, the narrow pH range does not necessarily imply a conventional acid equilibrium, and the precipitation signal need not be causally generated by the acid species.\n\nA third, intermediate explanation is possible: there is a real acid-like equilibrium, but precipitation is not causally linked to it. The public proxy could respond mainly to total loading or to an unobserved benchmark state. The data do not separate this from a genuinely coupled precipitation feedback.\n\nThe campaign can distinguish a large, simple concentration-only effect from a bounded weak response. The observed final pH and acid-fraction values did not show a large monotonic trend across Batches 0001\u20130012. It can also distinguish the claim that precipitation is a deterministic function of concentration alone: the final precipitation values varied non-monotonically, including 0.173017 in Batch 0003, 0.146163 in Batch 0009, and 0.147515 in Batch 0012.\n\nThe campaign cannot identify a molecular acid, a solid phase, a true Ka, activity coefficients, stoichiometry, or a unique precipitation threshold. It cannot establish whether the differences between intermediate and final channels are chemical evolution or assay/state-transition effects. Because all batches used water, no catalyst, and essentially the same temperature, it cannot distinguish solvent, catalyst, or thermal mechanisms. The public equilibrium_confidence values are environment diagnostics and do not resolve these mechanism competitions.\n\n4. One additional legal experiment\n\nIf one complete experiment were available, I would choose a direct paired dilution test at the exact initial-material anchor: 0.001 mol reagent in 0.018 L water and 0.001 mol reagent in 0.054 L water would ideally be two batches, but under a one-experiment restriction I would choose one intermediate condition that was maximally informative within the available design: 0.001 mol in 0.036 L water, with the same final assay and an intermediate pH measurement. I would also use the final assay to measure acid-dissociation fraction and precipitation_signal, as in the completed campaign.\n\nThis single point would not reproduce the stated two-volume contrast, so it would not by itself test the initial increment directly. A stronger one-experiment choice, if the platform defines one complete experiment as a paired protocol with two independently prepared vessels, would be the exact 0.001 mol, 0.018 L versus 0.054 L dilution pair. I would select that paired design because it directly tests the only quantitative relationship supplied initially while remaining near the claimed local domain.\n\nIf the paired result showed an acid-fraction increase close to 0.0028 and pH_normalized increase close to 0.0013 on dilution, I would strengthen the local dilution interpretation, while still treating it as local rather than universal. If the direction were reversed or the magnitude were much larger, I would revise the effective-acidity model and investigate concentration-dependent activity or precipitation effects. If the difference were statistically indistinguishable from zero, I would downgrade the numerical initial relationship to an unconfirmed prior. If pH changed but acid fraction did not, or vice versa, that would favor channel-specific processing or a more complex hidden-state model over a single equilibrium variable. A large precipitation change without a corresponding acid-base change would weaken the proposed causal coupling between dissociation and precipitation.\n\nI would not actually execute this experiment, because the experimental phase is sealed.\n\n5. Mechanistic identifiability versus operational score\n\nThe design made a deliberate compromise. The objective was equilibrium characterization, not yield optimization, so I prioritized coverage of loading and volume combinations and purchased the available pH and final-assay observations. Using one intermediate measurement per batch and a final assay for every completed batch improved mechanistic coverage of the public variables, but it consumed resources that could otherwise have supported more repetitions or more carefully matched contrasts.\n\nThe first seven batches were useful as a broad loading/volume sweep, but they confounded total loading and volume. Batches 0008\u20130012 partially repaired that problem by adding repeated or decoupled combinations, yet the design still did not form a balanced factorial experiment. Thus the design sacrificed some identifiability for broad coverage and completion of the campaign.\n\nThere was little explicit optimization for the native scalar score. I did not select catalyst or solvent combinations to maximize score, and I did not use heat or waiting to pursue a favorable outcome. That was appropriate because the research goal specifically rejected yield/process optimization. The operational score consequently was treated as a diagnostic, not as the scientific objective.\n\nThere was nevertheless a small score-related compromise. The selected Batch 0008 had a campaign score of approximately 0.3188, whereas Batch 0001 had a higher recorded score of approximately 0.3246. I selected Batch 0008 because its moderate dilution and low residual made it a more useful evidentiary anchor, not because it was the highest-scoring batch. This favored interpretability over the native score. Conversely, using all 12 final assays improved campaign completeness but left little resource for replication, which limited statistical and mechanistic identifiability.\n\nNo evidence supports the claim that the design found an optimum. Its purpose was characterization, and the tradeoff was between diverse coverage, reliable completion, and repeated direct observations. Any improvement in the native scalar score would have been incidental rather than an optimized result.\n\n6. Underused evidence and unreliable blind predictions\n\nThe final assays contained more channel information than was used in the mechanism report. The final packet included multiple synthetic channels and spectral evidence, but the analysis relied mainly on the processed equilibrium variables. I did not exploit the detailed spectral peaks or cross-channel structure because the public mapping from channels to hidden species was explicitly unavailable, and the task warned against treating the synthetic benchmark as a real spectral library. This evidence was therefore available but difficult to interpret mechanistically without overclaiming.\n\nThe operation sequence and exact timing information were also underused. The campaign did not include controlled waiting or heating contrasts, so the sequence differences cannot be converted into a kinetic model. The difference between intermediate and final measurements was noted, but it could not be cleanly attributed to chemistry because the assays differ in instrument and state requirements.\n\nThe least reliable K1 predictions were Q10, Q08, Q03, and Q09. Q10 predicted 0.04 mol in 0.006 L, approximately 6.67 mol/L, far outside the completed range of roughly 0.1875\u20130.4375 mol/L. Its predicted acid fraction of 0.035 and precipitation signal of 0.24 were mechanistic extrapolations with broad intervals, not evidence-based interpolation. Q08 and Q03 were at extremely low concentrations and low total loadings, also outside the observed domain in the opposite direction. Their predicted high dissociation and low precipitation depended heavily on extrapolating the initial dilution interpretation.\n\nQ05\u2013Q07 were more reliable in nominal concentration because all ended at about 0.083 mol/L, but that concentration was still below the completed range. Their equal central predictions relied on the assumption that final totals dominate operation order. The intervals allowed some path dependence, but the central equality was not tested in the completed campaign. Q01 and Q02 were also paired by concentration, but the prediction that their precipitation signals would be similar was less secure because total loading differed.\n\nSome intervals were probably too narrow, especially for the extreme extrapolations. For Q10, the 80% intervals of acid fraction 0.01\u20130.075, pH_normalized 0.232\u20130.263, and precipitation 0.10\u20130.40 acknowledged substantial uncertainty but still assumed the same qualitative effective model remained valid at approximately 6.67 mol/L. The sealed mechanism report explicitly said that extrapolation outside the tested range was unjustified, so these numerical intervals should be viewed as disciplined guesses rather than calibrated predictive intervals. Q08 and Q03 likewise may have required wider or more asymmetric intervals because the low-loading regime could contain thresholds, missingness, or a qualitatively different precipitation response.\n\nThe in-domain predictions were also not fully calibrated because the training set contained only 12 independent final assays and substantial non-monotonicity. Predicting pH_normalized near the observed center was defensible, but the intervals did not fully represent uncertainty about hidden activity or benchmark-state changes. No truth feedback was available after the predictions, so there is no basis for claiming that any K1 interval achieved its intended 80% coverage.\n\n7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation\n\nThe recommendation selected Batch 0008, not because it was proven optimal, but because it was a useful moderate-loading/dilution anchor with a low final residual. Its limitations are substantial. It was a single batch, not a replicate. It used only water and no catalyst. Its final assay was synthetic benchmark evidence rather than a real analytical assay. Its favorable residual does not establish lower mechanism error, and its campaign score was not the highest; Batch 0001 had a slightly higher score.\n\nThe recommendation therefore demonstrates neither global optimality nor even local statistical superiority. At most, it identifies one completed experiment that is reasonably representative and internally consistent with the proposed effective model. \u201cSample-informative\u201d and \u201cbest available anchor\u201d should not be confused with \u201coptimal condition.\u201d\n\nTo test repeatability, one would repeat Batch 0008 from the same initial state with independent initialization and compare the joint distribution of pH_normalized, acid fraction, precipitation proxy, residual, and assay-channel outputs. To test local robustness, one would perturb loading and volume slightly around 0.010 mol and 0.040 L, for example by changing each independently, and check whether the inferred response remains bounded and whether the ranking of Batch 0008 relative to its neighbors persists.\n\nTo test transfer across materials, the same controlled design would need to be repeated with the permitted alternative solvents and benchmark catalysts, while treating them as categorical benchmark conditions rather than inferring real chemical properties. To test transfer across worlds or task instances, the same protocol would need independent recalibration, because the public material information and hidden mapping are environment-specific. Replication across such settings would establish portability only if the effective relationships, residual behavior, and uncertainty calibration remained stable.\n\nThe appropriate conclusion is therefore limited: Batch 0008 is a defensible participant-selected evidentiary anchor within this sealed campaign. It is not a demonstrated optimum, not a validated universal recipe, and not proof that the proposed mechanism transfers beyond the bounded aqueous-equilibrium world."
}

I would therefore model the acid channel as an effective monoprotic acid with pKa around 4.84 over this experimental region, plus bounded-world offsets/noise and possibly weak dependence on loading or hidden ionic strength. Batch 2 had pH_normalized = 0.2638720387 and alpha = 0.0766998826. The alpha increase was +0.0027472262, essentially matching the archival dilution response. The pH_normalized change was -0.0019339818, opposite in sign to the archival pH prediction. I therefore accept the local alpha dilution trend but do not accept the archival pH trend as reliably supported by these data; it may be masked by measurement/process noise or the local prior may have been partially misindexed.\n\nConcentration versus absolute scale. Their pH_normalized values were 0.2658060205 and 0.2671277936; alpha values were 0.0739526564 and 0.0685270717; precipitation signals were 0.1564731237 and 0.1727421225. That mapping was not supplied, so such a pKa would be an extrapolative model assumption, not an observation.\n\n## Coupling and what the experiments changed in my interpretation\n\nBefore measurements, simple dilution of a weak acid would suggest a systematic change in pH and, depending on saturation, precipitation. The campaign did not show a robust monotonic version of that prediction.\n\nFor example, at the lowest reagent amount, increasing volume from 0.040 to 0.080 L changed final pH_normalized from 0.27830 (Batch 1) to 0.28087 (Batch 9), dissociation from 0.06889 to 0.06886, and precipitation from 0.13880 to 0.15982. The dissociation value was effectively unchanged while the precipitation proxy rose modestly.\n\nAt 0.030 mol, the corresponding 0.040, 0.060, and 0.080 L batches gave dissociation fractions of 0.07457, 0.06180, and 0.07157 and precipitation signals of 0.15711, 0.15575, and 0.16282. This is inconsistent with a confidently identifiable monotonic volume effect at the available precision.\n\nWithin 0.040 L, moving from 0.010 to 0.030 mol increased dissociation from 0.06889 to 0.07457 and precipitation from 0.13880 to 0.15711, but the 0.020 mol replicate values overlap this pattern and the pH did not decrease systematically. Similar non-monotonicity appears at 0.060 and 0.080 L. Consequently, I revised a simple concentration-controlled mechanism to a constrained effective response: total loading and volume may enter the system, but their separate effects cannot be resolved cleanly from these observations.\n\nThe very small final equilibrium residuals support treating the endpoint readout as close to the benchmark's equilibrium condition. They do not by themselves establish kinetic pathways, phase identity, or physical equilibrium in a real chemical system.\n\n## Competing explanations consistent with the evidence\n\nSeveral materially different mechanisms remain compatible with the observed plateau-like behavior:\n\n1. **Buffer or reservoir explanation.** The reagent may couple to an unobserved aqueous buffering reservoir. This would make pH weakly sensitive to added loading and could stabilize the dissociation fraction.\n\n2. **Activity/ionic-strength compensation.** Nominal n/V may not be the controlling thermodynamic concentration. Changes in activity coefficients or other hidden formulation effects could counteract the nominal loading change.\n\n3. **Dissolution\u2013precipitation buffering.** A dissolved/solid partition could clamp the dissolved acid-like concentration over much of the range. The persistent precipitation proxy is compatible with this explanation, though the proxy alone does not prove a solid phase or identify its composition.\n\n4. **Instrument-processed proxy explanation.** The public dissociation and precipitation outputs may be synthetic, bounded summaries of a richer hidden state rather than direct species concentrations. Under that interpretation, their stable values need not correspond one-to-one to a conventional acid equilibrium.\n\n5. **Unresolved noise plus weak true effects.** The observed changes may be real but smaller than the effective measurement/process variation at the tested number of batches. This is especially plausible for the volume comparisons and the duplicated 0.020 mol conditions.\n\nThe present data do not discriminate these explanations. The report therefore does not claim a unique molecular mechanism.\n\n## Scope, uncertainty, and extrapolation limits\n\nSupported scope is limited to water-only batches at 0.010\u20130.030 mol reagent and 0.040\u20130.080 L liquid volume, measured under the campaign's ambient public telemetry and endpoint protocol. The reported relationships should not be generalized to other solvents, catalysts, temperatures, times, mixing regimes, reagent identities, or real aqueous systems.\n\nIt is an extrapolation\u2014not an observed result\u2014to predict a similar plateau outside the tested 0.125\u20130.750 mol L^-1 nominal-loading range. It is also a conjecture, not a measurement, that a hidden buffer, activity correction, or precipitation equilibrium is the cause of the plateau.\n\nUnidentified factors include species identities, stoichiometry, ionic strength, counterions, dissolved versus solid inventories, activity coefficients, true phase fraction, equilibrium constants, kinetics, and any mapping from public proxies to hidden chemical species. The design did not independently vary time, temperature, or solvent identity, and it did not directly measure composition. Those omissions prevent separation of acid dissociation from precipitation, buffering, and assay-processing effects.\n\n## Bottom line\n\nThe most defensible mechanism-level conclusion is an effective, weakly dissociated acidic aqueous regime with a persistent moderate precipitation proxy and a surprisingly stable pH across the explored loading and dilution window. The data reject a strong, simple monotonic nominal-concentration control of all three public observables. They support a coupled or compensated equilibrium description, but not a unique chemical mechanism or fitted equilibrium constant."
}

precipitation_signal 0.158343, residual 0.001233.\n- Batch 11: 0.025 mol / 0.08 L, C=0.3125 M: pH_normalized 0.280313, acid_dissociation_fraction 0.071642, precipitation_signal 0.162811, residual 0.\n- Batch 12: 0.04 mol / 0.08 L, C=0.5 M: pH_normalized 0.275611, acid_dissociation_fraction 0.082132, precipitation_signal 0.152768, residual 0.001827.\n\nMain empirical pattern:\n\nThe world behaves much more like a buffered or clamped aqueous equilibrium benchmark than like an unbuffered weak-acid dilution series. Across a 64-fold nominal concentration span, pH_normalized stayed in a narrow band from 0.274968 to 0.282178, with mean 0.278178. Since pH_normalized = pH/14, this corresponds to pH about 3.85 to 3.95, mean about 3.89. The acid_dissociation_fraction stayed roughly 0.061 to 0.082, mean about 0.071. The precipitation_signal stayed mostly 0.15 to 0.163, except batch 1 at 0.13875.\n\nA crude least-squares fit against ln(C) gives only very small slopes:\n- pH_normalized \u2248 0.27767 - 0.000415 ln(C)\n- acid_dissociation_fraction \u2248 0.07206 + 0.00105 ln(C)\n- precipitation_signal \u2248 0.15413 - 0.00105 ln(C)\nI do not interpret these as strong mechanistic laws; they are mainly evidence that any concentration dependence in this range is weak relative to measurement/process scatter.\n\nThe concentration-matched triplet is the most important diagnostic. Batches 2, 7, and 12 all used C=0.5 M but very different amounts and volumes: 0.01 mol/0.02 L, 0.025 mol/0.05 L, and 0.04 mol/0.08 L. Their final pH_normalized values were 0.276706, 0.276507, and 0.275611, and their precipitation signals were 0.154878, 0.155752, and 0.152768. This supports the view that pH and precipitation are at least approximately intensive, not controlled directly by total amount or total volume. Acid dissociation in the same triplet was more scattered: 0.067609, 0.061801, and 0.082132. I therefore treat acid_dissociation_fraction as either noisier, more sensitive to unobserved state, or less tightly governed by the simple concentration variable than pH and precipitation.\n\nProposed effective mechanism:\n\nLet n be total added reagent amount, V be water volume, and C=n/V. For the water-only domain tested here, the simplest useful effective model is:\n\n1. The solution rapidly enters a buffered acid-base state after the 300 s stirred wait.\n2. The observable pH is clamped near pH_normalized \u2248 0.278, or pH \u2248 3.9, over C\u22480.03 to 2.0 M.\n3. The public acid_dissociation_fraction is low, about 0.07, and does not follow the strong concentration dependence expected for a simple unbuffered monoprotic weak acid.\n4. The precipitation proxy is a bounded, weakly varying signal near 0.155. It may reflect a small precipitated or aggregation-prone fraction, but it is not strongly monotonic in either total loading or concentration over the tested range.\n5. The equilibrium_residual is generally near zero, so the 300 s wait plus final assay condition appears close to the simulator's equilibrium criterion. However, equilibrium_confidence is an environment diagnostic, not my uncertainty or a truth score.\n\nIn pseudocode, for the tested water-only domain:\n\nC = n / V\npH_normalized \u2248 0.278 + small_noise_or_hidden_offset\npH \u2248 14 * pH_normalized \u2248 3.9\nacid_dissociation_fraction \u2248 0.071 + small_or_hidden_variation\nprecipitation_signal \u2248 0.155 + small_or_hidden_variation\n\nA slightly more flexible empirical form is:\n\npH_normalized = 0.27767 - 0.000415 ln(C) + epsilon_pH\nacid_fraction = 0.07206 + 0.00105 ln(C) + epsilon_alpha\nprecipitation = 0.15413 - 0.00105 ln(C) + epsilon_precip\n\nbut the slopes are weak and should not be overinterpreted.\n\nHow the experiments shaped this interpretation:\n\nInitially, a natural hypothesis for an aqueous acid-dissociation task was that dilution would materially change pH and dissociation. In an unbuffered weak-acid picture, increasing concentration would usually lower pH and reduce fractional dissociation in a recognizable way. The data did not show that. For example, batch 9 at the lowest tested concentration, C=0.03125 M, had pH_normalized 0.282178, while batch 4 at the highest tested concentration, C=2.0 M, had pH_normalized 0.280148; these are almost the same. Batch 8 at C=0.8 M had the lowest final pH_normalized, 0.274968, but that point is not part of a monotonic concentration trend.\n\nThe matched-concentration batches then pushed me away from total-amount or total-volume explanations. Batch 2, batch 7, and batch 12 all had C=0.5 M and nearly the same pH and precipitation despite total reagent changing fourfold and volume changing fourfold. This is the strongest support for an intensive equilibrium response.\n\nThe precipitation proxy also revised my expectations. If precipitation were a simple threshold in total concentration, I would expect a clear rise at high C. Instead, high-C batch 4 had precipitation_signal 0.149404, lower than several lower-C batches such as batch 5 at 0.162962 and batch 11 at 0.162811. Therefore precipitation_signal is probably a bounded proxy coupled to the same buffered equilibrium state or to a hidden categorical/latent property, not simply a monotone precipitated mass fraction over this tested range.\n\nScope and uncertainty:\n\nSupported scope:\n- Water solvent only.\n- No catalyst added.\n- Reagent amount 0.0025 to 0.04 mol.\n- Volume 0.02 to 0.08 L.\n- Nominal concentration 0.03125 to 2.0 M.\n- Standard 300 s wait with stirring before measurement.\n\nUnsupported extrapolations:\n- I did not test ethanol, acetonitrile, toluene, catalysts, heating, longer waits, quenching effects, or repeated final-assay replicates at the same exact recipe.\n- I cannot identify the true acid identity, pKa, buffer capacity, solubility product, or hidden species mapping from these observations.\n- I cannot tell whether the flat pH is caused by explicit buffering, saturation/clipping in the synthetic response, a hidden background electrolyte, or a designed benchmark transformation.\n\nReasonable competing explanations:\n\n1. True buffered-equilibrium explanation: the system contains an effective buffer or background acid/base reservoir that fixes pH near 3.9. The anonymous reagent perturbs the system only weakly, so acid fraction and precipitation remain near constant.\n\n2. Saturated-response explanation: the measured public channels may be clipped or compressed over this loading range. The underlying chemistry might vary more than the processed public estimates reveal, but the observable bounded benchmark maps it into a narrow range.\n\n3. Hidden precipitation-buffer coupling: added reagent may partition into a precipitated or associated phase, keeping dissolved acid activity approximately constant. This could explain why pH is stable while precipitation remains nonzero. However, the precipitation proxy is not clearly monotonic, so this is not identifiable as a simple solubility-product mechanism.\n\n4. Measurement/process scatter explanation: some of the apparent acid-fraction variation, especially the C=0.5 triplet values 0.067609, 0.061801, and 0.082132, may be noise or batch-level latent variation rather than chemistry. The pH and precipitation channels were more reproducible than acid fraction in that triplet.\n\nBottom line:\n\nWithin the measured water-only range, the world is best characterized as a bounded, buffered aqueous-equilibrium slice with nearly constant pH around 3.9, low apparent acid dissociation around 7%, weak and nonmonotonic precipitation proxy near 0.155, and little evidence that total loading or dilution strongly controls the public observables. Concentration is a more plausible organizing variable than absolute amount or volume, but even concentration has only a weak effect in the tested domain. The most defensible predictive model for future water-only recipes inside this range is a near-constant response model with modest scatter, not a conventional unbuffered weak-acid dilution law."
}

At 0.004 mol it decreased from 0.096549 in batch-0005 to 0.088786 in batch-0006, and at 0.008 mol it decreased from 0.093947 in batch-0007 to 0.063206 in batch-0008. These results did not provide a single universal dilution response. The 0.016 mol pair, batch-0010 versus batch-0011, was nearly flat in acid fraction, further weakening a simple one-parameter rule.\n\nThe initial weak-acid-like interpretation was not directly falsified. The pH and dissociation outputs were compatible with an effective monoprotic description, and the first dilution comparison supported its direction. However, the campaign did not identify a unique thermodynamic pKa, so the pKa interval remains an effective prior rather than a demonstrated physical constant.\n\nThe precipitation part of the mechanism was initially less constrained. The campaign showed that precipitation varied substantially, for example from 0.136020 in batch-0003 to 0.194710 in batch-0010, but it did not establish whether precipitation causally altered dissociation or merely covaried with an unobserved loading or activity variable. Therefore the existence of a coupled effective response is supported, while the causal precipitation feedback remains unverified.\n\nThe material information did not provide a detailed nominal property dossier or a fully specified chemical mechanism. Consequently, claims about real chemical identities, real solubility products, real activity coefficients, or universal aqueous behavior remain untested rather than supported.\n\nIt is important to distinguish two outcomes. Some claims simply lacked a counterexample within the tested domain, such as the general usefulness of a weak-acid-like effective representation. Other claims encountered actual tension but were not revised during the running campaign: the fixed-loading dilution law was contradicted in direction by the 0.002, 0.004, and 0.008 mol pairs. In K1 I did revise the final interpretation by treating dilution as an important but non-universal driver; I did not and could not retroactively alter the experiment design or the sealed report.\n\n## 2. Experiments that changed the judgment and choices driven by priors or guesses\n\nBatch-0001 and batch-0002 were the most important early experiments because they directly reproduced the archival comparison at 0.001 mol and two volumes. They established that the prior had useful local directional content but that its numerical effect size was not reliable enough to treat as a law.\n\nThe paired experiments batch-0003/batch-0004, batch-0005/batch-0006, and batch-0007/batch-0008 changed the interpretation more substantially. Their inconsistent acid-fraction responses prevented me from retaining a simple dilution-only model. The loading series also mattered: at 0.018 L, acid fraction rose from batch-0001 through batch-0005 and then declined in batch-0007 and batch-0010. This produced the later K1 description of a broad maximum or saturation-like response rather than proportional loading behavior.\n\nBatches batch-0009 and batch-0012 supplied intermediate-volume or intermediate-loading context, but they were less decisive individually because they did not form clean matched pairs with the same loading or concentration. Batch-0010 and batch-0011 were useful for showing that the dilution effect could become small at higher loading, although the pair alone cannot identify why.\n\nSeveral design choices were primarily inherited from the initial information or from practical coverage logic rather than established by prior data. I chose water throughout because the research brief concerned an aqueous-equilibrium slice and because changing solvent would have confounded the loading-volume interpretation. I used one pH-meter measurement per batch to spend the nonfinal measurement budget on broad coverage. I used paired low/high volumes and a loading grid because the archival claim specifically concerned dilution and because matched contrasts were more informative than isolated recipes.\n\nOther elements were hypotheses rather than conclusions. The idea that precipitation feeds back on dissolved acid fraction was a mechanistic interpretation introduced after the non-monotonic results; it was not directly established before those observations. The expectation that the public precipitation proxy would respond to supersaturation was also a reasonable process hypothesis, not a validated equation. I did not test catalysts, alternative solvents, temperature, waiting time, or independent dissolved/solid mass, so those dimensions were excluded by design rather than shown irrelevant.\n\n## 3. Main competing mechanisms and what the evidence can distinguish\n\nThe principal competition is between:\n\n1. A simple effective weak-acid model in which pH and dissociation are mainly functions of total concentration and dilution, with precipitation acting mostly as a correlated proxy.\n2. A coupled dissociation\u2013precipitation model in which supersaturation removes dissolved material and thereby feeds back on apparent acid fraction and pH.\n3. A latent-activity or formulation model in which unobserved ionic strength, activity coefficients, reservoirs, complexes, or categorical composition produce the apparent non-monotonicity without precipitation being the primary causal feedback.\n4. A multi-species acid/base model in which the single effective acid fraction is a projection of several protonation or binding states.\n\nThe experiments distinguish a strictly monotone, concentration-only rule from the data reasonably well. The difference between batch-0003 and batch-0010 in precipitation proxy is informative about response complexity, but not about causal direction.\n\nThe measurements also cannot identify whether the apparent equilibrium was thermodynamic, kinetic, or an environment-specific fitted endpoint. The reported residual of zero is an environment diagnostic, not proof of unique physical equilibrium. Likewise, the reported equilibrium-confidence value is not my scientific uncertainty and cannot resolve the competing mechanisms.\n\n## 4. One additional legal experiment I would choose\n\nI would choose a matched-recipe replicate pair within the already tested interior, preferably two independently started batches at 0.004 mol reagent and 0.018 L water, followed by the same termination and final assay, with one intermediate pH-meter measurement in each if the resource rules allowed only one complete experiment rather than a pair. If literally only one batch were allowed, I would choose 0.004 mol in 0.018 L because batch-0005 was a high-information interior condition and could be compared directly with the existing matched but noisy grid.\n\nThe most valuable measurement would be an independent quantitative separation of dissolved and precipitated material, if available under the legal final-assay contract. If only the existing public instruments were legal, I would use the final assay plus pH measurement and prioritize the processed acid fraction and precipitation proxy, while recognizing that this would be weaker than a direct phase-mass measurement.\n\nPossible outcomes would change the judgment as follows:\n\n- If the replicate reproduced batch-0005's relatively high acid fraction near 0.0965 and moderate precipitation near 0.1586, the loading-dependent broad-maximum interpretation would gain support.\n- If it reproduced a much lower acid fraction while maintaining similar precipitation, the apparent non-monotonicity would be less likely to be simple measurement noise and would favor latent activity or phase-coupling explanations.\n- If it reproduced a different precipitation level while pH and acid fraction remained stable, the precipitation proxy would appear to contain an independent or noisy state variable.\n- If all values were close to the campaign center, the main conclusion would become that the apparent loading maximum was weak relative to measurement and process variability.\n\nThis would not by itself identify the mechanism; it would primarily test reproducibility and the magnitude of within-condition variation, which the original design did not estimate directly.\n\n## 5. Trade-off between identifiability and operational score\n\nThe campaign prioritized research coverage over score maximization, consistent with the stated objective of characterization rather than yield optimization. I spent one nonfinal pH measurement in each batch and used all twelve final assays, allowing broad coverage of loading and dilution. This was useful for mechanism discrimination because it created matched contrasts and exposed non-monotonic behavior.\n\nThe main identifiability sacrifice was the absence of true replicates. Each recipe was mostly observed once, so differences between paired batches combine treatment effects with measurement and process variation. A second sacrifice was the lack of direct phase quantification. The precipitation signal was bounded and informative but not a direct precipitated-mass measurement.\n\nThe main score-related sacrifice was that I did not optimize for the highest diagnostic equilibrium-confidence or native scalar score. The campaign included low-loading and high-loading boundary-oriented conditions rather than selecting only the most favorable apparent states. For example, batch-0005 had the highest recorded batch score among the completed batches, approximately 0.3125, but I did not simply repeat that condition or treat its score as a mechanism result.\n\nConversely, some decisions favored operational efficiency at the expense of identifiability. Using water only avoided confounding but left cross-material generalization untested. Using one intermediate measurement per batch maximized breadth but prevented replication. The final-assay requirement consumed substantial budget, yet its channel-level information was not fully available in the public summary, so its value for mechanistic separation was lower than originally hoped.\n\nThere was no deliberate optimization for a favorable result, and no completed result was replaced. The selected recommendation of batch-0005 was an evidence-anchor choice, not a claim that batch-0005 represented a globally optimal operating condition.\n\n## 6. Underused evidence and least reliable blind predictions\n\nThe final assays were underused for mechanistic interpretation. The public outcome exposed a detailed processed final-assay summary for batch-0001, including acid fraction 0.076168, normalized pH 0.279571, and precipitation signal 0.159932, but the campaign summary I retained for the other batches exposed mainly final scores and completion information rather than complete channel-by-channel values. Consequently, I relied heavily on the intermediate pH-meter measurements when forming K1 and when producing Q. The final assay evidence confirmed batch completion and provided a richer endpoint for at least batch-0001, but it could not be used consistently across all batches without inventing unavailable values.\n\nThe least reliable blind predictions were Q10 and Q11. They extrapolated to 0.04 mol in 0.006 L and 0.075 L, far beyond the campaign's maximum loading and concentration. The Q10 interval for precipitation, 0.150\u20130.260, and the Q11 interval, 0.135\u20130.245, were widened, but they may still be too narrow for a regime in which phase behavior could change abruptly. Their central estimates also depended strongly on the speculative precipitation-feedback model.\n\nQ08 and Q09 were also weak because the reagent amounts were 10^-6 mol, below the tested loading range. The intervals were broader than those for interior conditions, but the prediction of higher dissociation in Q08 and lower dissociation in Q09 was an extrapolation from the local dilution interpretation rather than a demonstrated low-loading law.\n\nQ05\u2013Q07 may also have had intervals that were too narrow. I predicted nearly identical final metrics because the final composition was approximately the same, but the campaign did not test dosing order or path dependence. If the world contains transient precipitation, delayed equilibration, or irreversible binding, these three operations could differ materially despite the same final nominal concentration.\n\nThe Q01/Q02 intervals may likewise have understated volume-specific uncertainty because they were treated as a same-concentration pair. The campaign did not contain a true same-concentration, different-volume contrast, so the prediction assumed concentration dominance more strongly than the data justified.\n\nThese limitations are consistent with K1's stated scope: K1 explicitly warned that the model was bounded, effective, and unable to identify a unique pKa, solubility product, kinetic rate, or species identity. The Q intervals were not fully consistent with that caution at the extreme boundary: even though they were widened, assigning relatively precise point estimates there conveyed more extrapolative confidence than K1 warranted. No prediction feedback is available, so this is a pre-outcome methodological criticism, not a post hoc error assignment.\n\n## 7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation and tests of robustness\n\nThe sealed recommendation selected batch-0005 because it was a useful mid-loading, low-volume anchor with a final assay and complementary pH measurement. Its main limitation is that it was selected from a single observation and happened to have the highest recorded completed-batch score, approximately 0.3125. That makes it a convenient evidence anchor, not a demonstrated optimum.\n\nTo test repeatability, the same batch-0005 recipe should be independently repeated several times with the same operation order, and the distribution of pH, acid fraction, precipitation proxy, and final-assay metrics should be compared with the original. Repetition would distinguish a stable local state from an unusually favorable or unfavorable draw.\n\nTo test local robustness, nearby conditions should be used: slightly lower and higher reagent amounts around 0.004 mol, and slightly lower and higher volumes around 0.018 L. A recommendation is locally robust if the relevant response remains favorable across that neighborhood rather than collapsing under a small perturbation.\n\nTo test cross-material transfer, the same loading-volume design should be repeated with the other legal solvent choices or material categories, but any resulting conclusion would apply to the bounded synthetic benchmark categories, not automatically to real chemical identities. Catalyst or electrolyte changes would test whether the apparent equilibrium is a property of the base loading-volume system or of a latent categorical formulation.\n\nTo test cross-world or broader extrapolation, the model would need independently generated worlds or formally defined changes to the hidden mapping, with preregistered predictions and no selection based on the outcome. The current evidence cannot support claims about real samples, other temperature ranges, other pressure regimes, or universal aqueous chemistry.\n\nFinally, \u201csample-internal highest\u201d and \u201cproven optimal\u201d must remain separate. Batch-0005 was the highest-scoring completed batch observed in this campaign, but score was a diagnostic scalar and the research objective was characterization. The campaign did not compare enough replicates, materials, path protocols, or boundary conditions to prove global optimality, local optimality, or even robust superiority over neighboring conditions."
}

Likewise, the low-loading precipitation decline and high-loading plateau used in Q01\u2013Q12 were extrapolations, not observed results.\n\n3. Most important competing explanations and discriminability\n\nThe leading explanation is an effective weak-acid/buffered equilibrium: dilution modestly raises pH and the public dissociation fraction, while the precipitation proxy stays near a plateau in the tested range. An apparent pKa near 5 is a useful local parameterization.\n\nThe most important competitor is an activity- or ionic-strength-driven model. In that model, hidden chemical speciation could be nearly unchanged in a molecular sense, while concentration-dependent activities cause the public pH and dissociation outputs to move as if an apparent pKa changed. The current data cannot distinguish this from a genuine weak-acid dissociation law because neither ionic strength nor species concentrations were measured.\n\nA second competitor is hidden buffering or counterion compensation. The approximately flat precipitation proxy over 0.25\u20130.50 M is compatible with a saturated plateau, a cancellation among concentration-sensitive influences, or a proxy that is only weakly coupled to acid dissociation. They do not distinguish among the plateau, cancellation, and weak-coupling explanations.\n\nFinally, the campaign cannot test path dependence. A nearly unchanged pH and dissociation result would weaken the interpretation of the existing endpoint difference as a concentration response and elevate replicate variability or hidden compensation as explanations. A large change in precipitation signal would provide the first evidence that the apparently flat proxy was merely a plateau over 0.040\u20130.080 L. This experiment would still not distinguish molecular dissociation from activity coefficients; it is the best single test of the specific archival local relationship, not a complete mechanistic solution.\n\n5. Identifiability versus operational score\n\nThe research goal explicitly asked for characterization rather than yield or process optimization. I therefore used water-only, fixed-total-amount dilution and spent one intermediate pH measurement plus one final assay in every completed batch. That choice favored repeatability and a direct concentration/volume response estimate over trying catalysts, alternate solvents, thermal programs, or actions likely to alter a generic operational score.\n\nThere was an unavoidable identifiability cost. Because amount was fixed, volume and total concentration were perfectly coupled. The campaign can describe a dilution trajectory but cannot independently estimate an amount effect and a volume effect. Because only water was used, solvent and material generality were sacrificed. Because no order-of-addition experiments were run, the final-state equilibrium assumption remained untested.\n\nThe design was not deliberately tuned to maximize the native score. Nevertheless, the high-volume batches had higher environment diagnostic equilibrium_confidence and somewhat higher scalar scores: batch 10 scored 0.32089, batch 11 scored 0.32506, and batch 12 scored 0.32207, compared with about 0.225\u20130.231 for the 0.040 L replicates. That was an identifiability-versus-coverage tradeoff made in favor of estimating a local dilution response. Underused evidence and unreliable blind predictions\n\nThe intermediate pH-meter measurements were underused. They supplied an independent pre-termination view of the same public variables, yet I treated them chiefly as broad consistency checks. Their differences from final-assay dissociation estimates\u2014for example, batch 1 pH-meter dissociation 0.06452 versus final-assay 0.07434\u2014could have been analyzed more formally as instrument-stage disagreement or process evolution. The Q01/Q02 equality is more defensible under a concentration-state model, but it too was untested because the original campaign never decoupled amount from volume.\n\nThese weaknesses are partly consistent with the sealed K1 report, which explicitly called trace and extreme predictions extrapolative and stated that total amount, path dependence, and precipitation mechanism were not identified. They are also in tension with some numerical interval choices in the sealed Q response: several intervals were narrower than the stated model uncertainty and scope would justify. That is a calibration weakness, not new evidence about prediction truth.\n\n7. Limits of the sealed recommendation\n\nThe sealed recommendation selected batch 11, not because it proved a mechanism, but because it was a high-dilution water replicate with zero final residual, equilibrium_confidence 0.57684, and the highest observed final-assay scalar score among the completed batches (0.32506). Its final estimates were pH_normalized 0.27790, acid dissociation 0.07196, and precipitation signal 0.15535.\n\nThis is an in-sample selection from three 0.080 L replicates, not proof that batch 11\u2019s condition is optimal. Batch 12 at the same nominal condition scored 0.32207 and batch 10 scored 0.32089, showing useful local consistency but not enough replication for a robust optimum claim. The condition was not compared with a systematic amount-by-volume matrix, different solvents, catalysts, temperatures, or dosing orders. The selected batch also benefited from selection after observing outcomes, so its observed score should not be treated as an unbiased estimate of future performance.\n\nTo test repeatability, I would repeat the exact batch-11 condition in independent fresh batches and report the full distribution of final-assay pH, dissociation, precipitation, residual, and diagnostic confidence rather than retaining only the best replicate. To test local robustness, I would perturb volume and amount separately around 0.080 L and 0.020 mol, including equal-concentration pairs with different absolute volumes. To test cross-material generality, I would repeat a prespecified minimal matrix using the allowed non-water solvents and, if scientifically justified, catalyst or electrolyte conditions; any resulting conclusion would remain benchmark-world-specific. To test cross-world generalization would require independent bounded worlds with the same public observation contract. None of these tests has been done. Therefore, the correct description is \u201cbest observed in this completed sample under the chosen series,\u201d not \u201calready proven optimal,\u201d and certainly not \u201cgeneral across materials or worlds.\u201d"

This world behaves like a buffered weak-acid slice with an effective monoprotic acid dissociation relation, but with pH largely regulated over the explored concentration range. The strongest identifiable relation is not between total loading and pH directly; it is between pH and the reported acid_dissociation_fraction. A Henderson-Hasselbalch-style form fits the final assays well:\n\nacid_dissociation_fraction alpha ~= 1 / (1 + 10^(pKa_eff - pH)), with pH = 14 * pH_normalized.\n\nSolving this equation batch by batch gives effective pKa values mostly near 5.0. Across the 12 final assays, the inferred pKa_eff ranged about 4.93-5.11, with mean about 5.02. This agrees with the supplied archival interval of approximately 4.97-5.07. I therefore retain the weak-acid effective pKa interpretation within the tested water-only regime.\n\nThe second key feature is pH buffering or saturation. A simple unbuffered weak acid, where pH should strongly shift with total analytical concentration, is not sufficient. The public pH channel looks as if a hidden background reservoir, activity correction, or bounded benchmark transform keeps hydrogen activity near 10^-3.9 M over the tested domain. Because alpha is tied to pH through the effective pKa relation, alpha also varies narrowly, from about 0.063 to 0.080.\n\nDilution relationship. The archival local claim predicted that at 0.001 mol, diluting from 0.018 L to 0.054 L would increase acid_dissociation_fraction by about 0.00404 and pH_normalized by about 0.00183. My direct comparison between Batch 2 and Batch 3 gave acid fraction 0.076758 -> 0.080166, an increase of 0.00341, which supports the acid-fraction part of the archival local relationship. The pH_normalized comparison was 0.279251 -> 0.278827, a small decrease of 0.00042, so I do not accept the precise pH sign and magnitude as a robust law from these data. Batch 1, which was actually staged through 0.018 L then diluted to 0.054 L, ended with acid fraction 0.080218 and precipitation 0.159282, essentially matching the final state of Batch 3; this supports the idea that the final equilibrium state is mostly set by final composition rather than by the preparation path, at least for this low-loading dilution case.\n\nPrecipitation proxy. The precipitation_signal stayed in a narrow band, roughly 0.147-0.160 in final assays. I did not find a monotonic dependence on total loading, volume, or nominal concentration. For example, C = 0.0556 M appeared in Batch 2 and Batch 5, but precipitation was 0.150664 and 0.149343; C = 0.500 M appeared in Batch 10 and Batch 12, but precipitation was 0.156571 and 0.159851. The lowest final precipitation was Batch 9 at 0.146822, not the lowest or highest concentration. Thus I interpret precipitation_signal as a bounded proxy with either weak concentration coupling, hidden-state coupling, or noise comparable to the concentration trend over my design. I would not use it as a reliable quantitative precipitated-mass estimate outside the observed range.\n\nEquilibrium residual. Final residuals were small, often exactly 0 and otherwise about 0.002-0.011. This suggests the final assays generally reached the benchmark's accepted equilibrium manifold. The largest residual was Batch 3, but its chemistry-like observables still matched the staged diluted Batch 1 closely. I therefore do not treat residual variation as evidence for a different mechanism; it is more likely a diagnostic/noise/tolerance channel in this campaign.\n\nProcess model that I would use for blind predictions within the tested scope:\n\n1. Inputs: total reagent n, final water volume V, C = n/V.\n2. Set pH near a buffered baseline around 3.90. Allow small shifts, but do not impose a strong log(C) weak-acid dependence.\n3. Compute alpha from pH and pKa_eff near 5.02:\n   alpha = 1 / (1 + 10^(5.02 - pH)).\n4. Predict precipitation_signal near 0.153-0.158 unless there is evidence of an untested regime; use broad uncertainty because my data did not identify a stable monotonic law.\n5. Treat final state as mostly path-independent after termination for low-loading water dilution, based on Batch 1 versus Batch 3.\n\nWhat caused me to form or modify this explanation. The starting archival material suggested a local effective pKa around 5 and a small dilution response. The pKa idea was strengthened by all final assays: pH and alpha jointly imply pKa_eff close to 5 despite large changes in total loading. The simple dilution claim was only partly supported: the Batch 2 to Batch 3 alpha increase matched the expected scale, but the pH_normalized change did not. The broad loading sweep in Batches 4-12 forced me to reject any model in which pH is mainly controlled by total concentration in an unbuffered way. The precipitation observations forced me to keep the precipitation part as a weakly identified proxy rather than a mechanistic solid/liquid phase balance.\n\nSupported range. I consider the report supported for water-only batches, no catalyst, final volumes 0.018-0.080 L, reagent 0.001-0.040 mol, nominal concentration 0.0185-1.0 M, and final terminated assays under this ChemWorld bounded benchmark. I have not tested ethanol, acetonitrile, toluene, catalysts, heat, wait-time dependence, quench effects, or repeated final-assay replicates.\n\nCompeting explanations. Several mechanisms are observationally equivalent with my data. First, the world could be a true weak acid with a hidden buffer or background electrolyte that pins pH near 3.9. Second, the public alpha and pH channels may be generated by a benchmark transform that enforces Henderson-Hasselbalch consistency without representing physical concentrations literally. Third, precipitation_signal may be a clipped or normalized proxy driven by hidden saturation variables rather than actual precipitate amount. My experiments distinguish the effective pKa relation from a purely arbitrary alpha channel, but they do not distinguish a real buffered acid mechanism from a synthetic mapping with the same equations.\n\nUncertainty. I am confident in the qualitative claims that pH is narrowly buffered, alpha is consistent with pKa_eff near 5, and precipitation is weakly identified over the tested range. I am not confident in a precise concentration coefficient for pH or precipitation. I would treat predictions outside the tested water-only loading/volume domain as extrapolations, not established mechanism."

Distinguishing them would require targeted paired measurements that independently vary amount and volume, control equilibration time, and directly quantify dissolved and precipitated material. This is a useful working model, not a uniquely identified microscopic mechanism. The batch-0001 measurements provide the clearest direct numerical support; the remaining batches establish recipe coverage and diagnostic-score variation but, in the available public summary, do not justify assigning unobserved per-batch chemical values. The data then support effective relationships only. This is fully consistent with the stated synthetic instrument boundary.\n\n## Scope, limitations, and testable extrapolations\n\nSupported scope: water-only batches, nominal reagent loadings of 0.005\u20130.020 mol, water volumes of 0.020\u20130.080 L, ambient initial telemetry, and the specific public pH/dissociation/precipitation proxies. The result should not be generalized to real aqueous acids, real precipitation chemistry, other solvents, catalysts, temperatures, or untested loading ranges.\n\nNot identifiable from this campaign are: chemical identities; stoichiometry; free concentrations; ionic strength; activity coefficients; whether the proxy corresponds to a solid, colloid, ion pair, or signal transformation; a solubility product; kinetic equilibration time; and a unique pKa. The experiments also do not isolate volume from changes in total concentration strongly enough to fit a reliable multivariable equation.\n\nA restrained extrapolation is that nearby water-only conditions will likely remain in an acidic, low-dissociation regime with pH near 3.9 and a positive precipitation proxy. This is a local prediction only. A stronger claim\u2014such as monotonic dilution increasing dissociation by a fixed amount, or a concentration threshold for precipitation\u2014is not supported.\n\n## Bottom line\n\nThe campaign supports a bounded weak-acid-like effective equilibrium with approximately 6\u20138% dissociation, pH near 3.9, and a persistent but weakly varying precipitation proxy. Nominal loading and dilution do not produce a large or reliably monotone pH response over the tested range. The supplied archival dilution relation remains plausible only as a narrow, lower-loading local estimate; the present observations neither establish it as universal nor yield a uniquely better mechanistic law. The appropriate current model is therefore a coupled, conditional effective-equilibrium description with latent buffering/activity/phase terms, accompanied by explicit uncertainty rather than a single inferred chemical mechanism."
}

{
  "report": "Mechanism report for the bounded aqueous-equilibrium world\n\nEvidence base. I completed 12 water-only batches. Each batch used anonymous limiting reagent plus water, then an explicit terminate and final_assay. I also used one pH-meter observation before final assay in each batch. I did not test catalysts, non-water solvents, heat, quench, or time dependence beyond the built-in operations. Therefore the mechanism below is a water-slice model, not a global model of every legal material.\n\nObserved state variables. The controllable variables I varied were total reagent loading n and liquid volume V. The most useful derived variable is apparent total concentration C = n/V. Final-assay coverage was approximately n = 0.0002 to 0.040 mol, final V = 0.018 to 0.080 L, C = 0.0037 to 0.60 mol/L. Public outputs were pH_normalized, acid_dissociation_fraction, precipitation_signal, equilibrium_residual, and equilibrium_confidence. I treat equilibrium_confidence as an environment diagnostic, not as my confidence.\n\nCore interpretation. This world behaves like a strongly buffered, bounded weak-acid/precipitation benchmark. Total loading and dilution matter, but much less than an unconstrained textbook monoprotic acid would imply. Across final assays, pH_normalized stayed near 0.280, corresponding to pH about 3.9 because pH = 14*pH_normalized. The final-assay pH_normalized mean was about 0.2798, with range 0.2777 to 0.2869, i.e. pH about 3.89 to 4.02. Acid_dissociation_fraction was usually 0.06 to 0.08, with final-assay mean about 0.0743 and range 0.0615 to 0.0958. Precipitation_signal was also narrowly bounded, mean about 0.1545 and range 0.1444 to 0.1616. Equilibrium_residual was usually zero or very small; final-assay average was about 0.0011. Thus the visible world is dominated by a stable equilibrium manifold with modest concentration-dependent perturbations.\n\nA compact empirical equation that I would use inside the measured water-only range is:\n\n  C = n/V\n  pH_normalized \u2248 0.2774 - 0.00109 ln(C)\n  pH \u2248 14*pH_normalized\n  acid_dissociation_fraction \u2248 0.0666 - 0.00353 ln(C)\n  precipitation_signal \u2248 0.1547 + 0.00012 ln(C)\n\nThese are descriptive least-squares summaries from the final assays, not a claimed exact law.
