Batch 1 was designed to test the supplied archival dilution anchor: 0.001 mol in 0.018 L water was measured by pH_meter, then diluted to 0.054 L and final-assayed. The pre-dilution pH_meter gave pH_normalized 0.282119, acid_dissociation_fraction 0.080664, precipitation_signal 0.174337. The post-dilution final_assay gave pH_normalized 0.279045, acid_dissociation_fraction 0.072658, precipitation_signal 0.144393. Taken literally, that within-batch comparison moves opposite to the archival direction for pH and dissociation, but it is confounded by instrument change and terminal/final-assay context. I therefore did not accept it as a clean falsification by itself.\n\nThe broader matrix clarified the picture. Batch 2 final assay repeated 0.001 mol at 0.018 L and gave pH_normalized 0.279238, acid 0.070028, precipitation 0.154038. Batch 3 used 0.003 mol diluted to 0.054 L, giving the same nominal final concentration as batch 2, and produced pH_normalized 0.278882, acid 0.063176, precipitation 0.146175. The pH agreement between batches 2 and 3 supports concentration as a major public descriptor, while the acid and precipitation differences warn that there is noise, batch/instrument variation, or a weak dependence on total loading separately from C.\n\nDilution-pair evidence was mixed but consistent with only a small effect. For 0.003 mol, batch 3 final at 0.054 L had pH_normalized 0.278882, acid 0.063176, precipitation 0.146175, while batch 4 final at 0.018 L had pH_normalized 0.279416, acid 0.071430, precipitation 0.154879. For 0.006 mol, batch 5 final at 0.054 L had pH_normalized 0.277929, acid 0.079667, precipitation 0.157415, while batch 6 at 0.018 L had pH_normalized 0.280470, acid 0.073223, precipitation 0.159723. For 0.024 mol, batch 9 final at 0.080 L had pH_normalized 0.277729, acid 0.078975, precipitation 0.149130, while batch 10 at 0.040 L had pH_normalized 0.279587, acid 0.061528, precipitation 0.154086. These pairs do not support a large monotone dilution law; they support a small concentration effect embedded in measurement/process scatter.\n\nThe low-loading edge was informative. Batch 12 used 0.0002 mol in 0.054 L, the lowest concentration tested. It had the highest final pH_normalized, 0.286872, and highest final acid_dissociation_fraction, 0.095824. This is qualitatively consistent with weak-acid dilution: at very low total loading, a larger fraction is dissociated and the solution is less acidic. However its precipitation_signal was 0.161586, not reduced, so the precipitation proxy is not simply proportional to total precipitated mass.\n\nPrecipitation interpretation. The public precipitation_signal appears to be a bounded proxy coupled weakly to the equilibrium state rather than a direct amount of solid. It remained close to 0.15 across concentrations that varied by more than 100-fold. It sometimes decreased with dilution in a pair, as in batch 1 post-dilution 0.144393 and batch 9 0.149130, but batch 12 showed high precipitation_signal at the lowest concentration. I would model it as a clipped diagnostic such as\n\n  precipitation_signal = clip(P0 + small terms in alpha, pH, C, and hidden batch state + noise, 0, 1)\n\nrather than as a solubility-product mass balance. A true solubility threshold may still exist, but it was not separately identifiable from these data.\n\nWeak-acid consistency and pKa. The public material information mentioned an archival effective pKa interval near 4.61-4.71. If I combine the mean final pH about 3.917 with mean acid_dissociation_fraction about 0.074 using a textbook Henderson-Hasselbalch form alpha = 1/(1+10^(pKa-pH)), the implied pKa is about 5.01. This mismatch suggests that either the pH and dissociation outputs are calibrated proxies rather than exact thermodynamic quantities, or there are hidden activity/buffer/ionic-strength transformations in the benchmark. I therefore would not force a strict physical pKa model. The safer mechanism is an effective bounded acidity model with a local pKa-like parameter that depends on calibration and possibly concentration.\n\nReasonable generative process. My best process-level explanation is:\n\n  1. Add water and anonymous reagent; total concentration C = n/V is computed.\n  2. The system rapidly maps C onto a buffered acid-equilibrium manifold.\n  3. pH is held near 3.9 by an effective background/buffer term; dilution moves it only weakly upward.\n  4. The apparent dissociated fraction is centered near 0.07; it tends to rise at very low C but with substantial scatter.\n  5. A precipitation proxy is generated from the same hidden equilibrium state but is clipped/normalized, producing a near-constant value around 0.15 over this design space.\n  6. The equilibrium_residual reports how well the internal benchmark solver/state matches its equilibrium manifold; it was mostly near zero, so most batches were internally self-consistent.\n\nSupported scope. I am comfortable applying this description to water-only batches with reagent loading 0.0002-0.040 mol, final volume 0.018-0.080 L, and concentration 0.0037-0.60 mol/L, without catalysts or heating. Interpolation within that region should expect pH_normalized around 0.278-0.287, acid_dissociation_fraction around 0.06-0.10, precipitation_signal around 0.14-0.16, and small equilibrium_residual. Extrapolation outside this region, especially to other solvents, catalysts, time/temperature changes, or much higher/lower concentrations, is speculation.\n\nUnidentified factors. I could not distinguish measurement noise from true hidden batch effects because the 12-batch budget allowed only sparse overlap. I did not isolate final_assay versus pH_meter calibration differences: batch 1 showed a large apparent drop after dilution, but that comparison also changed instrument and terminal state. I did not identify whether total loading n has a separate effect beyond C, because same-C comparisons were limited. I did not identify the physical meaning of precipitation_signal. I also did not test whether the process is time dependent or whether catalysts/solvents alter the effective acidity manifold.\n\nCompeting explanations. One equivalent explanation is a pure lookup/response-surface benchmark in C with no mechanistic acid chemistry; the weak-acid language may just be an interpretation of calibrated channels. Another is a buffered weak acid with hidden ionic-strength/activity corrections that make pH almost invariant and decouple the reported acid fraction from direct hydrogen concentration. A third is a two-regime model: most points lie on a flat buffered plateau, while very dilute cases such as batch 12 enter a higher-dissociation, higher-pH regime. The current data support the plateau-plus-weak-dilution view but do not uniquely choose among these explanations.\n\nBottom line. The world is not a yield-optimization system and not an ordinary unbuffered acid solution. It is best characterized as a bounded, buffered aqueous equilibrium proxy: concentration and dilution have detectable but small effects; the supplied local dilution relationship is plausible in direction but too strong and not cleanly reproduced by my direct batch-1 observations; precipitation is a normalized coupled diagnostic rather than a directly interpretable mass of solid; and the reliable prediction envelope is narrow, water-only, and empirical."
}

  "report": "1. Initial claims: supported, contradicted, and untested\n\nThe initial public material did not provide a substantive local mechanistic estimate. Therefore there was no supplied relationship that could be meaningfully confirmed or refuted. The material catalog did establish that the selected materials were bounded benchmark formulations and that the synthetic instruments were not real-world predictive devices; those scope claims remained supported.\n\nThe main mechanistic claim developed in K1 was an effective weak-acid/precipitation picture: total loading and dilution affect an acid-base partition, while a coupled but distinct precipitation process responds to the dissolved state. This was supported only in a limited phenomenological sense. Batch 1 showed a nonzero dissociation estimate and nonzero precipitation proxy together: the intermediate measurement gave acid_dissociation_fraction 0.076740 and precipitation_signal 0.200479, while the final assay gave 0.075178 and 0.150764. That co-occurrence is consistent with the proposed picture, but it does not identify a molecular acid-base mechanism.\n\nThe distinction between acid-base observables and precipitation was also supported as an observation-level statement. In Batch 1, pH and dissociation changed relatively little between intermediate and final measurements, whereas precipitation_signal changed from 0.200479 to 0.150764. K1 correctly treated this as evidence that the precipitation channel was not identical to the acid-base channel. It did not establish whether the difference was physical evolution, sampling, or instrument-layer behavior.\n\nThe claim that the response was not simply monotonic in loading was only weakly supported. The final-assay scores ranged from 0.224877 in Batch 6 to 0.320753 in Batch 3, with several higher-loading batches scoring lower than Batch 3. However, the score is composite and is not a direct precipitation or dissociation measurement. This was evidence against using a simple score-as-loading law, not strong evidence against monotonic behavior in any individual mechanistic variable.\n\nSeveral stronger claims remained untested. The campaign did not identify the reagent, acid/base species, solid phase, activity coefficients, precipitation stoichiometry, or equilibrium constant. It also did not directly test time dependence, mixing dependence, order of addition, or a controlled same-composition comparison with different histories. K1 acknowledged these limitations. There was no clear case in which a mechanistic claim had already been contradicted and was knowingly left uncorrected; rather, most claims were deliberately stated as effective hypotheses with limited support. The strongest distinction is therefore between \u201cno direct disproof was found\u201d and \u201cthe mechanism was demonstrated\u201d: the former applies to the proposed model, while the latter does not.\n\n2. Experiments that formed or changed the judgment\n\nBatch 1 was the most important single experiment for the initial mechanistic interpretation because it was the only batch whose detailed intermediate and final values were directly available in the working record. Its intermediate values were pH_normalized 0.292041, acid_dissociation_fraction 0.076740, precipitation_signal 0.200479, and equilibrium_residual 0.000000. Its final values were pH_normalized 0.288787, acid_dissociation_fraction 0.075178, precipitation_signal 0.150764, and equilibrium_residual 0.003634. The contrast between stable-looking pH/dissociation and a changing precipitation proxy formed the judgment that precipitation should be treated as a distinct coupled state rather than as a synonym for dissociation.\n\nThe loading series from Batches 2\u201312 changed the judgment from a possible simple monotonic story to a more cautious one. The nominal campaign covered 0.005\u20130.035 mol at mostly 0.060 L, with Batch 1 at 0.010 mol/0.050 L and Batch 12 at 0.015 mol/0.070 L. The score pattern did not increase steadily with loading: Batch 3 scored 0.320753, while Batches 6, 7, and 11 scored 0.224877, 0.237191, and 0.231781. This encouraged the K1 statement that loading could not safely be treated as a simple monotonic benefit. Because only composite scores were available for most of these batches in the retained context, the series could not strongly determine which individual mechanism caused the pattern.\n\nThe initial material information was important for scope and interpretation. It warned that the solvent names were selectable benchmark materials and that catalysts and reaction species were anonymous; the campaign therefore used water only and avoided real-chemical identity claims. The instrument contract also motivated treating equilibrium_confidence as an environment diagnostic rather than as personal confidence.\n\nSome choices were not strongly evidence-driven. Using one intermediate pH measurement and one final assay per batch was a reasonable coverage choice, but it was not derived from a validated time-course model. Using only water simplified the design and respected the aqueous-equilibrium goal, but it prevented testing material/formulation alternatives. The particular loading and volume grid was selected from the campaign budget and broad coverage considerations, not from a fitted response model. Selecting Batch 3 in K1 was participant-owned and was justified as a useful higher-loading evidentiary anchor; it was not based on a demonstrated mechanistic optimum. The decision to describe the system with weak-acid and precipitation equations was an effective modeling choice made after seeing Batch 1, not a conclusion already established before the experiment.\n\n3. Most important competing mechanism\n\nThe most important competitor is a latent response-surface or measurement-layer explanation. Under this view, pH_normalized, acid_dissociation_fraction, and precipitation_signal are correlated synthetic outputs of loading, volume, and hidden benchmark state, but they need not correspond to a separable chemical equilibrium followed by precipitation. The Batch 1 observations are compatible with this explanation because a synthetic channel can change independently of the others.\n\nA second competitor is a kinetic nucleation or aggregation mechanism. It could explain why the final precipitation proxy differs from the intermediate proxy while pH and dissociation remain similar. In this account, the apparent precipitation response depends on time, mixing, settling, or sampling history rather than on an equilibrium solubility condition.\n\nA third competitor is an activity or ionic-strength mechanism. Apparent dissociation changes could arise from activity corrections, screening, or hidden counterions, while the precipitation proxy responds to the same unobserved formulation variable. A concentration-only acid-base model would then be inadequate.\n\nThe existing experiments can distinguish some very broad possibilities. They can reject the idea that the reported final composite score is a reliable monotonic function of nominal loading, because the scores do not rise monotonically. They can also establish that the two measurement stages in Batch 1 did not produce identical precipitation values. They cannot distinguish true precipitation kinetics from assay-specific variation, nor can they establish that the dissociation channel is a literal species fraction. The campaign also cannot determine whether volume acts through dilution alone or through hidden activity, geometry, or phase effects. Same-composition order tests were proposed in the later Q set, but no truth feedback has been provided and those Q results were not available when K1 was written.\n\n4. One additional legal complete experiment\n\nIf one additional complete experiment were allowed, I would repeat the Batch 1 final composition\u20140.010 mol reagent in 0.050 L water\u2014but add a controlled time-history measurement before termination. I would measure with the pH meter after preparation, wait a declared fixed duration with fixed stirring, measure again, then terminate and perform the required final assay. The purpose would be to hold nominal loading and volume constant while testing whether the precipitation-related and acid-base channels drift with time.\n\nIf pH and dissociation remained stable while the precipitation proxy changed reproducibly during the wait, that would strengthen the kinetic or phase-relaxation explanation and weaken a purely instantaneous concentration-only model. If all channels remained stable and the final assay matched the intermediate result within the stated uncertainty, the Batch 1 discrepancy would be more plausibly assay noise or sampling variation. If pH and dissociation changed together with precipitation, that would support stronger coupling between acid-base partitioning and the evolving solid or dissolved state. If the result differed substantially from Batch 1 despite identical nominal inputs, that would reveal important stochastic, history-dependent, or instrument-layer variability and would substantially widen the uncertainty of K1 and Q.\n\nThis is a proposed design only. It was not executed, and no result should be inferred from it.\n\n5. Mechanistic identifiability versus operational score\n\nThe research goal explicitly prioritized characterization rather than yield optimization. That affected the design in several ways: the campaign used a spread of reagent amounts and volumes, included intermediate pH measurements, and used final assays for all 12 completed batches. The selection of Batch 3 in K1 was not presented as proof of an optimum; it was chosen as an evidentiary anchor within a loading spread.\n\nThere was nevertheless a real tradeoff. The use of one intermediate measurement per batch maximized coverage under the 12-measurement allowance, but it sacrificed within-batch temporal identifiability. A time series in fewer batches would have been better for distinguishing equilibrium from kinetics. Similarly, the broad loading grid improved response-surface coverage but left only limited replication at exactly matched compositions and volumes. The use of water only preserved the aqueous scope and reduced confounding, but it prevented testing whether the apparent relationships were material-specific.\n\nSome operational choices also indirectly protected score. Avoiding heating, catalysts, and risky operations kept safety risk low and avoided spending budget on variables outside the stated research goal. However, that was not score optimization in the ordinary sense; it was alignment with the characterization objective. There was no deliberate sacrifice of mechanistic identifiability to maximize leaderboard score, but the finite budget meant that coverage, repeated measurements, and temporal controls could not all be maximized simultaneously. Conversely, the design did not intentionally sacrifice score to pursue an elaborate mechanistic intervention; it stayed within simple, low-risk aqueous compositions.\n\n6. Underused evidence and unreliable blind predictions\n\nThe largest underused evidence was the detailed final-assay information from Batches 2\u201312. In the retained working context, only their final composite scores were visible, not their full per-channel pH, dissociation, precipitation, residual, and confidence values. Therefore the loading series could not be fit quantitatively, even though it was the most relevant evidence for concentration and dilution effects. The campaign's instrument artifacts may contain richer information, but no new artifact access or post hoc laboratory work was permitted here.\n\nThe intermediate measurement design was also underused for mechanism identification. Each batch had one pH-meter observation, but without repeated times or matched-history controls it could not determine whether the intermediate-to-final discrepancy in Batch 1 was temporal, procedural, or analytical. The final-assay composite scores were similarly difficult to use because they combine multiple channels and include a diagnostic equilibrium-confidence component.\n\nThe least reliable blind predictions were Q10 and Q11. Q10 proposed approximately 6.67 mol/L, far above the main campaign range, and Q11 proposed approximately 0.533 mol/L, also above it. Their predictions of lower normalized pH, low dissociation, and substantial precipitation were mechanistically plausible extrapolations, but the wide intervals still may have been too narrow because saturation, phase behavior, and synthetic boundary behavior were unknown. Q03, Q04, Q08, and Q09 were also difficult because their absolute loadings were far below the campaign range; the predicted near-zero precipitation could be too confident if the proxy has a nonzero baseline or if trace loading is amplified by an unobserved mechanism.\n\nQ05\u2013Q07 may also have had intervals that were too narrow. I predicted nearly identical values because their final nominal compositions were similar, but their order-of-addition histories were different. K1 had explicitly stated that order dependence and kinetics were unresolved. Therefore the close central predictions were reasonable as an equilibrium hypothesis, but the intervals should probably have been wider for precipitation, especially Q07, where reagent was added before final dilution.\n\nQ12 was the most defensible of the holdout predictions because its nominal concentration was interior to the campaign region, but even its interval relied on sparse channel-level calibration. The Q predictions were consistent with K1's stated scope in one important respect: they explicitly widened uncertainty for boundary extrapolations and warned that the benchmark was synthetic. They were not fully consistent with K1's uncertainty discussion in another respect: several intervals implicitly assumed a directional concentration trend that the campaign had not identified quantitatively. The principal weakness was not claiming certainty, but assigning directional point estimates and intervals without the full per-channel Batches 2\u201312 data.\n\n7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation\n\nThe sealed recommendation selected Batch 3 because it was a useful higher-loading anchor and had the highest observed composite score, 0.320753. Its limitation is that this is a sample-in-campaign selection, not proof of optimality. Batch 3 was not shown to maximize any individual mechanistic variable, and the composite score itself is not the research objective. The correct distinction is \u201chighest observed score among the completed batches\u201d rather than \u201cproven best condition.\u201d\n\nThe recommendation is also limited by sparse local replication. Batch 3 was not repeated at exactly the same reagent amount and volume with independent history, so its reproducibility is unknown. To test repeatability, one would repeat the same Batch 3 recipe with the same measurement sequence and compare all public channels, not merely the composite score. To test local robustness, one would perturb reagent amount and volume slightly around Batch 3 while keeping the measurement protocol fixed. A stable response surface would support local robustness; a sharp or irregular change would suggest threshold, phase, or history effects.\n\nCross-material generalization is especially unsupported. The campaign used water and did not test ethanol, acetonitrile, toluene, or the anonymous catalysts. Because the material information states that these are categorical benchmark effects rather than ordinary property-based predictions, Batch 3 cannot be assumed to transfer across materials. A cross-material test would require matched loading and volume recipes with the alternative solvent or formulation, followed by the same final assay. That would test transport and activity changes rather than merely repeating the same aqueous state.\n\nCross-world generalization is even weaker. The instrument contract defines a bounded synthetic benchmark and explicitly disclaims prediction of real samples or physical devices. Thus neither Batch 3 nor the K1 mechanism should be treated as a real-chemistry optimum. A different world could alter the latent mapping, noise, saturation, precipitation behavior, or meaning of the dissociation proxy.\n\nIn summary, the recommendation was appropriate as a participant-selected replay anchor because it represented a distinct interior-to-high loading condition and had the highest observed composite score. It was not a validated optimum, not a uniquely identified mechanism, and not evidence of cross-material or cross-world superiority."
}

Buffered weak-acid equilibrium: loading changes total concentration, but a buffer or conjugate reservoir holds pH nearly fixed; precipitation changes modestly with supersaturation.\n\nB. Activity-coefficient model: nominal concentration changes are substantially offset by ionic-strength-dependent activities, producing weak or nonmonotonic apparent pH and dissociation responses.\n\nC. Precipitation-feedback model: the system initially responds to loading, but removal of one effective species changes the subsequent acid equilibrium and masks the direct concentration effect.\n\nD. Synthetic observation-layer model: the latent chemical state may vary more than the reported pH and fraction because the public channels are bounded, noisy proxies with normalization or saturation.\n\nE. Hidden categorical state: even without deliberately varying catalyst or solvent, the benchmark may contain a latent support/electrolyte or batch-state variable that contributes to the observed scatter.\n\nThese explanations cannot be ranked decisively from the completed observations alone.\n\nScope and extrapolation\n\nThe supported scope is the tested bounded regime: water, no catalyst, reagent loadings 0.001\u20130.030 mol, liquid volumes 0.018\u20130.072 L, and the corresponding synthetic assay outputs. Interpolation within this region should be treated as uncertain and phenomenological. Extrapolation to higher loading, lower or higher volume, other solvents, catalysts, different temperatures, real chemical identities, or actual solid yields is not justified.\n\nA practical predictive representation for this world would use an empirical response surface with uncertainty:\n\n[y, alpha, P] = F(n_reagent, V, n_reagent/V, solvent, catalyst, latent_state) + measurement_error,\n\nwith monotonicity not imposed unless separately demonstrated. The current data support using pH and acid dissociation as jointly informative state indicators and precipitation_signal as a coupled but non-specific response. They do not support reducing the system to a single universal pKa, a linear dilution coefficient, or a uniquely determined precipitation equation."
}

The same endpoint can be generated by buffering, activity effects, precipitation feedback, or a hidden observation transform. It is not a demonstrated optimum, not a universal reference, and not evidence that the proposed mechanism is uniquely correct."

The precipitation quantity is a bounded public proxy, not a directly identified precipitate mass or concentration.\n\n| Batch | Water (L) | Total loading (mol) | Nominal loading/volume (mol L^-1) | pH_normalized | Acid dissociation fraction | Precipitation proxy | Equilibrium residual | Environment diagnostic: equilibrium_confidence |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| batch-0001 | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.333 | 0.291733 | 0.080128 | 0.147684 | 0 | 0.501392 |\n| batch-0002 | 0.030 | 0.030 | 1.000 | 0.292295 | 0.071032 | 0.154038 | 0 | 0.361684 |\n| batch-0003 | 0.045 | 0.010 | 0.222 | 0.286971 | 0.069410 | 0.149479 | 0 | 0.552539 |\n| batch-0004 | 0.045 | 0.030 | 0.667 | 0.291776 | 0.057403 | 0.154611 | 0 | 0.372979 |\n| batch-0005 | 0.060 | 0.010 | 0.167 | 0.293849 | 0.072129 | 0.167168 | 0.000293 | 0.510142 |\n| batch-0006 | 0.060 | 0.030 | 0.500 | 0.293684 | 0.072925 | 0.155365 | 0 | 0.368297 |\n| batch-0007 | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.333 | 0.288135 | 0.080614 | 0.160424 | 0 | 0.497602 |\n| batch-0008 | 0.045 | 0.030 | 0.667 | 0.291947 | 0.067507 | 0.145408 | 0 | 0.371129 |\n| batch-0009 | 0.060 | 0.010 | 0.167 | 0.290500 | 0.074907 | 0.142218 | 0 | 0.515926 |\n| batch-0010 | 0.030 | 0.030 | 1.000 | 0.292182 | 0.072397 | 0.158048 | 0 | 0.374858 |\n| batch-0011 | 0.045 | 0.010 | 0.222 | 0.292408 | 0.073920 | 0.154410 | 0 | 0.567238 |\n| batch-0012 | 0.060 | 0.030 | 0.500 | 0.292449 | 0.068180 | 0.160090 | 0 | 0.365314 |\n\nBatch-0011 was selected as the completed-experiment recommendation because it is a replicated low-loading/intermediate-volume condition and gave the largest final-assay equilibrium-confidence diagnostic (0.567238). This diagnostic is an environment readout, not a measure of my epistemic confidence.\n\n## 2. Direct empirical relationships\n\n### pH is nearly invariant over the tested matrix\n\nFinal pH_normalized values lie between 0.286971 and 0.293849, corresponding to pH about 4.02\u20134.11. Most values are close to pH 4.09. Within either loading level, changing water from 0.030 to 0.060 L does not show a consistent monotonic pH change. For example, at 0.030 mol, final pH_normalized is 0.292295, 0.291776, and 0.293684 at 0.030, 0.045, and 0.060 L, respectively.\n\nThis supports an effective buffered or self-regulated acidity response in this bounded slice, rather than a large dilution-driven pH excursion across the tested range. It does not establish that pH is exactly independent of volume.\n\n### Acid dissociation is low and broadly stable\n\nThe final acid-dissociation fraction ranges from 0.057403 to 0.080614. The six low-loading batches average approximately 0.0752 and the six high-loading batches approximately 0.0682. This is a small separation relative to the observed batch-to-batch spread and the stated final-assay noise scale for this channel. Accordingly, the data support a low effective dissociated fraction, roughly 0.07, but do not securely establish a loading effect on that fraction.\n\nAt a fixed loading, there is no reproducible volume trend. For example, the 0.030-mol series gives 0.071032, 0.057403/0.067507, and 0.072925/0.068180 at 0.030, 0.045, and 0.060 L. The duplicate values at 0.045 L themselves demonstrate appreciable local variation.\n\n### The precipitation proxy is approximately constant in this design\n\nThe low-loading group has mean final precipitation proxy approximately 0.1536; the high-loading group has mean approximately 0.1546. Individual values span 0.142218\u20130.167168, but neither volume nor total loading has a clear monotonic association. Therefore, the supported statement is only that this proxy remains at a moderate baseline level, near 0.15, under these water-only conditions.\n\n### Equilibrium residual is effectively zero at final assay\n\nEleven final assays reported residual 0; batch-0005 reported 0.000293. In the operational sense represented by this public residual, all twelve terminal states are consistent with equilibrium or a residual below meaningful resolution for this experiment.\n\n### Total loading strongly changes the environment's equilibrium-confidence diagnostic\n\nThis is the clearest group separation. At 0.010 mol, final diagnostic values are 0.497602\u20130.567238 (mean about 0.524); at 0.030 mol, they are 0.361684\u20130.374858 (mean about 0.369). Within each total-loading group, volume has little evident effect. This is a reliable empirical relationship for this environment diagnostic: the 0.030-mol condition produces a lower diagnostic value than 0.010 mol under the tested volumes.\n\nIt should not be converted into a chemical claim that high loading is \u201cless equilibrated.\u201d The near-zero final residuals show why that interpretation would be unwarranted. The diagnostic may instead encode a model-specific assessment of equilibrium quality, complexity, or uncertainty at the state being characterized.\n\n## 3. Effective chemical interpretation\n\nThe simplest effective description compatible with the public observations is a weak monoprotic-acid-like equilibrium embedded in a buffered or otherwise regulated aqueous background:\n\nHA \u21cc H+ + A\u2212\n\nwith an effective dissociation fraction\n\nalpha = [A\u2212] / ([HA] + [A\u2212])\n\nnear 0.07 in the observed states. If ideal Henderson\u2013Hasselbalch behavior is used only as a local descriptive approximation,\n\npH = pKa_eff + log10(alpha / (1 - alpha)),\n\nor equivalently\n\npKa_eff = pH + log10((1 - alpha) / alpha).\n\nRepresentative estimates from final observations are about 5.14 for batch-0001 (pH about 4.084, alpha = 0.080128) and about 5.30 for batch-0004 (pH about 4.085, alpha = 0.057403). Most of the data are compatible with a local effective pKa near 5.2, with substantial measurement/process scatter. This is not identification of a real acid, a thermodynamic standard-state pKa, or a universal reaction mechanism.\n\nA useful phenomenological model is therefore:\n\npH \u2248 pH0 + epsilon_pH,\nalpha \u2248 alpha0 + epsilon_alpha,\nP_proxy \u2248 P0 + epsilon_P,\nD_eq = g(total loading) + epsilon_D,\n\nwhere pH0 is about 4.09, alpha0 about 0.07, P0 about 0.15, and g decreases substantially between 0.010 and 0.030 mol. Over the tested range, a first practical approximation is that the direct volume coefficients in the first three equations are small compared with observed variation. This is an empirical local approximation, not a claim that the coefficients are physically zero.\n\nThe data also allow a coupled process in which acid-base speciation, an unobserved buffer/reservoir, and a solubility/aggregation process jointly determine the observables. In such a process, precipitation could remove or sequester some material while the pH remains buffered, producing a nearly constant precipitation proxy and low dissociation fraction. The present data do not identify which species, if any, precipitates, nor whether the proxy reflects actual solid formation, aggregation, saturation, or a synthetic mapping of several hidden states.\n\n## 4. Relationship to the supplied local archival estimate\n\nThe supplied archival estimate proposed an effective pKa interval of 5.149\u20135.249 and predicted, at 0.001 mol, a small dilution change from 0.018 to 0.054 L: delta pH_normalized = 0.001275 and delta dissociation fraction = 0.002776.\n\nThe present approximate pKa values are broadly consistent with that interval, though individual estimates extend slightly outside it. Thus the observations do not motivate rejection of the archival effective-pKa statement.\n\nHowever, the dilution prediction was not directly tested. My loads were 0.010 and 0.030 mol rather than 0.001 mol, and my volumes were 0.030\u20130.060 L rather than the archival 0.018\u20130.054 L anchor. Moreover, the predicted pH-normalized shift is small relative to the observed variation and stated measurement uncertainty. The correct conclusion is that the archival dilution relationship remains plausible but unconfirmed in its stated local domain; it cannot be validated, quantitatively revised, or extrapolated from this matrix.\n\n## 5. Why intermediate and final measurements were treated differently\n\nEach batch had a pH-meter reading before termination and a final assay. The pH-meter readings were directionally useful but varied more strongly in the dissociation and precipitation channels. For example, batch-0004 gave intermediate acid dissociation 0.094290 and precipitation 0.179955, versus final 0.057403 and 0.154611. I therefore base numerical conclusions on the consistent final-assay series rather than treating intermediate readings as independent confirmation of a fine-scale trend. Both measurements remain actual observations; the distinction is interpretive and reflects their different stated channel uncertainties and timing.\n\n## 6. Identifiability limits and competing explanations\n\n1. **Total amount versus concentration is not fully separable.** The high-total-loading conditions also have higher nominal loading/volume ratios than the low-total-loading conditions; there was no pair with matched concentration but different total moles. Thus the clear change in the equilibrium-confidence diagnostic could be caused by total moles, concentration, another state variable correlated with both, or the environment's diagnostic construction.\n\n2. **Volume effects are only bounded locally.** The absence of a clear trend from 0.030 to 0.060 L does not demonstrate dilution invariance at other volumes, lower loadings, different water compositions, or different temperatures.\n\n3. **No chemical identity or species balance is observed.** The anonymous reagent, acid species, counterions, buffer, and any solid phase were not compositionally resolved. A weak acid, a buffered polyprotic system, ion pairing, activity-coefficient changes, or a hidden coupled reaction can all yield similar effective alpha\u2013pH observations.\n\n4. **The precipitation signal is not a solubility measurement.** It supports only a stable public proxy around 0.15 in this regime. A true precipitation threshold, solubility product, solid identity, nucleation kinetics, and reversibility cannot be inferred.\n\n5. **The final state is not a kinetic experiment.** No time series, temperature series, or controlled waiting study was performed. Near-zero terminal residual does not identify the path, rate law, or time required to reach that state.\n\n6. **Non-aqueous and catalyst effects are out of scope.** Although other selectable solvents and catalysts exist in the material catalog, they were not tested. This report is specifically about the water-only bounded slice.\n\n## 7. Supported scope and careful extrapolations\n\nSupported within the tested water-only matrix:\n\n- Terminal pH is near 4.1 and changes little detectably with the tested water volumes and total loadings.\n- The effective dissociated fraction is low, near 0.07.\n- The precipitation proxy is near 0.15 without a resolved loading or dilution trend.\n- Final equilibrium residual is essentially zero in all twelve batches.\n- Raising total loading from 0.010 to 0.030 mol is associated with a strong drop in the environment's equilibrium-confidence diagnostic, while volume has little visible effect on that diagnostic within each loading group.\n- A local weak-acid-like effective pKa around 5.2 is compatible with the data and with the archival interval.\n\nReasonable but untested extrapolation:\n\n- If the same effective acid-buffer regime persists slightly beyond these conditions, pH and dissociation may remain only weakly dilution-sensitive. This is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated law.\n\nNot supported:\n\n- A universal aqueous pKa, a real molecular identity, a solubility product, a precipitation mechanism, a causal interpretation of the equilibrium-confidence diagnostic, or predictions for other solvents, catalysts, temperatures, or strongly different concentrations.\n\nOverall, the most defensible model is an effective, weak-acid-like and buffered aqueous equilibrium with low dissociation and a stable moderate precipitation proxy, plus a separate loading-dependent environment diagnostic. Several mechanistic realizations remain observationally equivalent under the completed experiment matrix."
}

Including the 0.030-mol conditions sacrificed operational score relative to the low-loading group but exposed the strong diagnostic group difference.\n\nThere was nevertheless an important identifiability failure: the matrix did not decouple total moles from concentration. The two total-load groups occupied non-overlapping concentration ranges. Thus the design made a useful loading contrast but not a causal loading test. A more identifiable allocation would have included matched-concentration/different-amount conditions and fixed-amount/different-volume conditions, especially near 0.001 mol.\n\nThere was no intentional sacrifice of identifiability merely to optimize score. Conversely, the replicate allocation did sacrifice coverage of the low-loading archival domain and order-of-addition histories for local repeatability. This was a reasonable but incomplete characterization trade-off, not proof of a mechanism.\n\n6. Underused evidence and the least reliable blind predictions\n\nThe intermediate pH-meter records were underused. K1 noted examples such as batch-0004, where intermediate acid dissociation was 0.094290 and final assay was 0.057403. These differences might contain information about measurement timing, sampling effects, or relaxation, but the experiment did not include a time-controlled design, and the instruments have different stated channel uncertainty. Treating them as direct kinetic evidence would have been speculative; ignoring them entirely also leaves potential information unused.\n\nThe local duplicate structure was only partly exploited. Batch-0003 versus batch-0011 and batch-0004 versus batch-0008 provide useful repeatability checks, but there were no duplicate pairs at every volume/loading cell. Consequently, uncertainty estimates in K1 were qualitative rather than a fitted variance model.\n\nThe least reliable blind predictions are Q10 and Q11, both involving 0.040 mol, beyond the completed maximum of 0.030 mol. Q10 is particularly weak because its nominal concentration is also far above the completed range. Its predicted precipitation estimate of 0.25 and 80% interval of 0.08\u20130.48 were explicitly mechanism-driven extrapolations, not data-supported threshold estimates. Q08 and Q09 are also weak because their 10^-6-mol trace loadings are several orders of magnitude below the study range.\n\nSeveral intervals were probably too narrow relative to K1's stated scope. In particular, Q01 and Q02 had narrow pH intervals despite being below the completed loading range; Q05\u2013Q07 used identical central predictions and intervals for different dosing histories despite K1 acknowledging that irreversible or history-dependent precipitation was untested. Q12, although closer to the measured domain, also inherited an optimistic narrow interval because the data did not establish a continuous response surface. These weaknesses are partly inconsistent with K1's stated uncertainty and scope, which explicitly rejected extrapolation to strongly different concentrations and untested histories. The blind prediction response did widen intervals at the extreme boundaries, but it should have widened them more uniformly whenever the query departed from the completed design.\n\n7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation\n\nThe sealed recommendation selected batch-0011 because it was a low-loading, intermediate-volume replicate with the highest observed final equilibrium-confidence diagnostic, 0.567238. This is a sample-in result: it is the highest observed diagnostic among the twelve completed batches. It is not a demonstration that batch-0011's recipe is globally optimal, chemically optimal, or even the expected best condition under repetition.\n\nIts main limitation is replicate context. Batch-0003 had the same nominal recipe and a lower but nearby diagnostic of 0.552539. That pair suggests local repeatability, but two observations cannot establish a robust mean, variance, or ranking against neighboring volumes and amounts. Selection on the largest observed value also creates ordinary winner's-noise risk.\n\nTo test repeatability, I would repeat the batch-0011 recipe independently several times with the same terminal assay and compare the distribution with batch-0003 and batch-0011. To test local robustness, I would perturb volume and amount slightly around 0.045 L and 0.010 mol while including matched-concentration and matched-amount controls. To test cross-material generality, I would vary solvent and catalyst only under a separately justified design; the completed water-only evidence does not support such transfer. To test cross-world generality, the entire matrix would need independent execution in another bounded world, because the present public channels and their mapping are world-specific.\n\nTherefore, \u201csample-in highest\u201d is true for batch-0011's observed diagnostic. \u201cProven optimal\u201d is not established for any operational, mechanistic, or transferable objective."
}

Therefore the initial local numerical claim was not directly verified.\n\nWhat was supported: the sign and small scale of a dilution/loading effect were broadly compatible with my observations. In the final-assay concentration fit I reported in K1, acid_dissociation_fraction decreased weakly with concentration, approximately acid_dissociation_fraction \u2248 0.0789 - 0.0193 C. That implies dilution should slightly increase the dissociation fraction, consistent with the initial prior. The pH effect was also small, consistent with the prior\u2019s small delta.\n\nWhat was contradicted or at least not physically validated: any interpretation of that pKa interval as an ordinary ideal monoprotic acid constant. In K1 I explicitly noted that \u201cthe reported pH and reported acid_dissociation_fraction are not mutually constrained in the way an ideal monoprotic acid in unbuffered water would require.\u201d Thus I found no reason to accept the initial pKa as a real thermodynamic parameter. This is not merely \u201cno counterevidence\u201d; it is a mismatch between the public channels and a simple physical weak-acid model.\n\nWhat remains untested: the exact low-loading dilution pair, temperature dependence, solvent identity effects, catalyst effects, and whether the initial relationship holds below my measured concentration range. My blind predictions Q01-Q04 and Q08-Q09 extrapolated into that low-loading region, but no truth has been returned, so those extrapolations remain unvalidated.\n\n2. Experiments that actually formed or changed my judgment\n\nThe 12-batch grid formed three main judgments in K1.\n\nFirst, the pH channel appeared buffered or compressed. This was driven by comparisons across the whole concentration span. In particular, batch 4 was the most concentrated measured endpoint, 0.035 mol in 0.040 L, C = 0.875 M, with final pH_normalized 0.291762. Batch 9 was the most dilute measured endpoint, 0.005 mol in 0.080 L, C = 0.0625 M, with final pH_normalized 0.290885. These were nearly identical despite a 14-fold concentration difference. That comparison was central to the K1 statement that the world behaves like a \u201cstrongly buffered bounded weak-acid/precipitation benchmark.\u201d\n\nSecond, the acid_dissociation_fraction judgment came especially from the 0.040 L series. Batch 1 at C = 0.125 M had final acid_dissociation_fraction 0.080542; batch 2 at C = 0.375 M had 0.071171; batch 3 at C = 0.625 M had 0.069169; batch 4 at C = 0.875 M had 0.057373. This monotone sequence caused me to accept a weak downward concentration trend. However, the 0.060 L and 0.080 L series were not comparably monotone, so I downgraded the claim to a weak effective relationship rather than a firm law.\n\nThird, the precipitation_signal judgment was changed by the lack of a clean trend. Batch 5, at only C = 0.083333 M, had final precipitation_signal 0.167108, while batch 8, at C = 0.583333 M, had 0.145406. Batch 4 at C = 0.875 M had 0.154614. These observations prevented me from claiming a strong precipitation threshold within the measured range. In K1 I wrote that precipitation was \u201ceffectively flat around 0.15 with batch-to-batch variation larger than the fitted slope.\u201d\n\nSome experimental choices depended more on the initial prior and my own design assumptions than on already observed data. The whole 3\u00d74 water-only concentration grid was chosen before observing campaign results, using the prior that dilution and loading were likely relevant. I did not adaptively add solvent/catalyst/temperature tests because the campaign was planned as a concentration-volume grid under limited final assays. The decision to use ph_meter once per batch was also based on the assumption that intermediate pH/dissociation readings would help identify equilibrium behavior; in practice, the final_assay values were more useful for the endpoint model.\n\n3. Current competing mechanisms and what the data can or cannot distinguish\n\nThe most important competing explanations are the same ones I named in K1, but they deserve sharper separation.\n\nA. Concentration-only equilibrium model. In this view, final observables depend primarily on C = n/V. This is attractive because it explains the broad dilution/load framing and supports why Q05-Q07 were predicted identically: they have the same final amount and volume. The data weakly support this for acid_dissociation_fraction, especially in the 0.040 L series.\n\nB. Separate amount and volume effects. In K1 I noted that fitting amount and volume separately could mimic a dilution effect without being strictly C-only. My 3\u00d74 grid is not strong enough to decisively distinguish n/V from separate n and V terms because amount and concentration are correlated within each volume series. The blind queries Q01/Q02 and Q03/Q04 were designed by the evaluator to test concentration-volume decoupling, but I do not yet know their outcomes.\n\nC. Buffered pH with synthetic diagnostic channels. This is the explanation I favored in K1. It says pH_normalized, acid_dissociation_fraction, and precipitation_signal are public processed observables in a bounded simulator, not necessarily a physically coupled acid solution. The observed inconsistency between pH and acid_dissociation_fraction under ordinary weak-acid equations supports this explanation.\n\nD. Hidden threshold or latent-state precipitation. My data cannot distinguish a truly flat precipitation baseline from a threshold lying outside the tested range. Since all measured precipitation_signal values clustered near 0.14-0.17, the campaign did not cross a strong precipitation boundary if one exists.\n\nE. Path dependence versus endpoint equilibration. I assumed path independence for simple water/reagent operations in Q05-Q07. My own campaign did not actually test different operation orders leading to the same final composition. Therefore this remains unresolved.\n\nThe existing experiments distinguish ordinary unbuffered acid chemistry from a bounded/buffered synthetic response fairly well. They do not distinguish concentration-only from separate amount-volume dependence, nor do they establish whether precipitation has a hidden high-concentration threshold.\n\n4. One additional legal complete experiment I would choose\n\nIf allowed one more complete experiment, I would choose a path-equivalence and low-loading calibration condition close to the blind-query decoupling region, for example:\n\nadd_solvent water 0.040 L; add_reagent 0.0006 mol; terminate; measure final_assay.\n\nThis is essentially the Q02 condition, C = 0.015 M. I would choose it because it directly probes the initial archival low-loading regime while staying within legal operation bounds and connects to Q01/Q02-style concentration-volume decoupling. If I could choose only one, I would prioritize this over another high-concentration point because my K1 report explicitly left the archival low-loading claim only indirectly tested.\n\nPossible outcomes and how they would change my view:\n\nIf pH_normalized remained near 0.293 and acid_dissociation_fraction near 0.079-0.085, it would support my K1 low-concentration extrapolation and strengthen the buffered endpoint model.\n\nIf pH_normalized rose substantially above the measured range, for example above 0.305, or acid_dissociation_fraction rose much above 0.10, it would show that my measured grid missed a low-loading regime and that my Q01-Q04/Q08-Q09 prediction intervals were probably too narrow.\n\nIf precipitation_signal dropped strongly toward zero at trace loading, it would suggest that the measured 0.15 proxy was not a constant baseline but a loading-dependent response whose low-end threshold I failed to sample.\n\nIf the result differed sharply from Q01-like concentration-equivalent behavior, that would support separate volume/amount terms rather than a concentration-only model.\n\nI would not actually execute this experiment now; this is only a retrospective design choice.\n\n5. Tradeoff between mechanism identifiability and operational score\n\nThe research goal was characterization, not yield optimization. My design mostly sacrificed operational score optimization for identifiability. I spent all 12 complete experiments on a broad water-only loading/volume grid instead of searching for a high-score condition. For example, batch 6 later had the highest observed leaderboard_score among my completed experiments, about 0.323128, but I did not know that in advance and did not exploit it with local replicates or neighboring optimization runs. I recommended batch 6 as an evidentiary anchor, not as a proven optimum.\n\nThe main identifiability gain was that the 3\u00d74 grid allowed me to see pH compression, weak dissociation trends, and precipitation flatness. The main identifiability loss was that I used no solvent, catalyst, wait-time, temperature, or path-order variation. I also did not include true replicates at the same final composition, so I had to infer noise from cross-condition scatter and ph_meter/final_assay disagreement.\n\nThere was little evidence that I optimized at the expense of mechanism. If anything, I sacrificed possible score by testing low and high loadings across a grid, including conditions that produced lower score, such as batch 4 and batch 8 around 0.232. However, I did sacrifice some mechanistic breadth by staying within water-only conditions. That was a deliberate narrowing of scope to address the stated acid-dissociation/dilution goal under a 12-final-assay limit.\n\n6. Evidence underused or difficult to use; least reliable blind predictions\n\nThe ph_meter observations were underused because they were difficult to reconcile quantitatively with final_assay. They provided intermediate pH/dissociation/precipitation estimates, but their acid_dissociation_fraction and precipitation_signal values sometimes diverged strongly from final endpoints. In K1 I cited batch 7, where ph_meter acid_dissociation_fraction was 0.111300 but final was 0.080564, and batch 6, where ph_meter was 0.047540 but final was 0.073091. I used them mainly as qualitative checks, not as equal-weight data. A more formal model could have used ph_meter-final differences to estimate observation noise or endpoint shift.\n\nThe equilibrium_confidence values were also hard to use. They varied substantially, for example batch 6 final equilibrium_confidence 0.568513 versus batch 8 0.371153, but the instructions warned that equilibrium_confidence is an environment diagnostic, not my uncertainty and not a task score. I therefore did not treat it as a mechanistic dependent variable. That was probably appropriate, but it means some public variation remained unexplained.\n\nThe least reliable blind predictions were Q10 and the trace/low-loading extrapolations Q03, Q04, Q08, and Q09. Q10 was far outside my measured range: 0.040 mol in 0.006 L gives C about 6.67 M, compared with my maximum measured 0.875 M. I gave Q10 wide intervals, but even those may be too narrow if clipping, precipitation thresholds, or nonlinear saturation dominate.\n\nQ03, Q04, Q08, and Q09 were also outside the measured loading range, especially Q08 and Q09 at 1e-06 mol. In K1 I stated that my model applied only to 0.005-0.035 mol and 0.040-0.080 L in water, so predicting trace amounts required extrapolation. My prediction intervals for these low-loading cases may have been too narrow, particularly for precipitation_signal, because I assumed a low-concentration buffered asymptote rather than allowing a collapse of precipitation toward zero.\n\nQ05-Q07 are unreliable for a different reason: they test operation-order/path dependence. In my predictions I explicitly assumed endpoint path independence after termination. K1 did not prove that; it only proposed it as an effective process picture. Therefore identical predictions for Q05, Q06, and Q07 could be overconfident if the simulator retains path memory.\n\nThere is some tension between my K1 scope statement and the blind predictions. K1 correctly warned that the model was water-only and valid only over my measured loading/volume range. Several blind predictions went outside that range. I did mark them as extrapolations in the rationales, but some intervals, especially for low-loading trace cases, may still not fully reflect model-form uncertainty.\n\n7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation and how to test it\n\nThe sealed recommendation selected completed experiment 6: 0.015 mol in 0.060 L, C = 0.250 M. My rationale at the time was that it was a central, non-edge condition with both ph_meter and final_assay observations, useful as an evidentiary anchor. It also happened to have the highest observed leaderboard_score in my campaign, about 0.323128, but I did not claim it was globally optimal.\n\nThe limitation is that batch 6 is a single observation. It is not a replicate-verified optimum, and it is not even necessarily the best local condition. Nearby measured points include batch 10 at C = 0.1875 M with score about 0.303886 and batch 11 at C = 0.3125 M with score about 0.309855. Batch 6 may reflect a real favorable region, measurement noise, or an unmodeled volume/amount interaction. Calling it \u201csample-internal best\u201d would be fair; calling it \u201cproven optimal\u201d would not.\n\nTo test repeatability, I would rerun the exact batch 6 recipe multiple times: water 0.060 L, reagent 0.015 mol, terminate, final_assay. That would estimate process and measurement variance for the selected condition.\n\nTo test local robustness, I would perturb amount and volume around it while holding either C or one primitive variable fixed: for example 0.012-0.018 mol at 0.060 L, and concentration-matched conditions such as 0.010 mol in 0.040 L or 0.020 mol in 0.080 L. This would reveal whether batch 6 is part of a broad plateau or a narrow accidental peak.\n\nTo test path robustness, I would compare one-shot dosing with split dosing at the same final n and V, similar to the logic behind Q05-Q07.\n\nTo test cross-material scope, I would repeat the same amount/volume condition in ethanol, acetonitrile, and toluene if legal and scientifically relevant, while recognizing that the material information warned solvent effects are benchmark categorical effects, not real solvent-property predictions.\n\nTo test cross-world or cross-seed generality, the same design would need to be replayed in independent ChemWorld instances. My current recommendation is only supported inside this sealed campaign world and should not be treated as a universal recipe."

Changes in amount and volume produced only small shifts relative to the observed pH level.\n\n2. **The acid-dissociation fraction is low but nonzero, approximately 0.06\u20130.08 in the tested water-only conditions.**\n\n   Increasing nominal reagent amount from 0.010 to 0.030 mol at 0.040 L reduced the condition mean from about 0.075 to 0.068. The analogous comparison at 0.080 L reduced it from about 0.073 to 0.067. This supports a weak, loading-dependent suppression of the effective dissociated fraction.\n\n3. **Dilution has a small and not cleanly identifiable effect on dissociation in this range.**\n\n   Doubling volume from 0.040 to 0.080 L at 0.010 mol changed the mean terminal acid fraction from about 0.0752 to 0.0729; at 0.030 mol it changed from about 0.0681 to 0.0665. These are small decreases, not a clear dilution-driven increase. Their magnitude is comparable with batch-to-batch variation, so I do not regard the sign as firmly established.\n\n4. **Dilution slightly raises pH in the observed slice, especially at higher nominal amount, but the effect is small.**\n\n   At 0.030 mol, doubling volume changed mean pH_normalized from about 0.2897 to 0.2927. At 0.010 mol the corresponding change was from 0.2907 to 0.2919. This is directionally compatible with dilution reducing effective acidity, but it is not sufficient to specify a universal pH-versus-concentration law.\n\n5. **The public precipitation proxy remains near 0.15 and has no strong, separable dependence on dilution.**\n\n   Its condition means span only about 0.152\u20130.157. The high-loading conditions were modestly higher than the low-loading conditions at 0.040 L, but this pattern weakened at 0.080 L. There is no evidence here for a sharp solubility threshold, a precipitation transition, or a dominant precipitation-controlled pH response within the tested range.\n\n6. **The equilibrium residual is close to zero in all completed final assays.**\n\n   Values were 0 to 0.007563, consistent with the runner returning a near-equilibrated public state rather than a large observable kinetic departure. The diagnostic confidence varied substantially by condition, with its clearest pattern being lower values at the higher amount and smaller volume. That diagnostic pattern may be useful for operating the benchmark, but it does not itself establish a chemical mechanism.\n\n### A compact effective model\n\nA conservative phenomenological description is:\n\n\\[\n\\alpha_{obs} \\approx \\alpha_0 - a\\,n - b\\,\\log(V/V_0) + \\epsilon_{\\alpha},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{pH}_{obs} \\approx \\mathrm{pH}_0 + c\\,\\log(V/V_0) - d\\,n + \\epsilon_{pH},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nP_{obs} \\approx P_0 + e\\,n + f\\,\\log(V/V_0) + \\epsilon_P,\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(n\\) is nominal added reagent amount, \\(V\\) is liquid volume, \\(\\alpha_{obs}\\) is the public acid-dissociation fraction, and \\(P_{obs}\\) is the public precipitation signal. In the tested region, the data support \\(a>0\\) weakly, \\(c>0\\) weakly, and a small positive loading contribution to \\(P_{obs}\\); they do not identify the signs or values of the remaining terms reliably.\n\nA chemistry-shaped interpretation of the same effective model is a weak monoprotic-acid-like equilibrium coupled to nonideal loading effects and a weak precipitation/removal channel:\n\n\\[\nHA \\rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\alpha \\approx \\frac{1}{1 + 10^{pK_{a,eff}-\\mathrm{pH}}},\n\\]\n\nwith \\(pK_{a,eff}\\) allowed to depend on concentration, ionic environment, or an unobserved condensed-phase partition:\n\n\\[\npK_{a,eff}=pK_a^\\circ+g(C,I,P,\\ldots).\n\\]\n\nIf the reported pH and dissociation fraction are treated literally as a single ideal monoprotic equilibrium, representative low-loading/low-volume batches imply an apparent effective pKa around 5.1\u20135.2. This is an **effective transformation of the public observables**, not an identified thermodynamic pKa: the experiment did not independently measure activity, ionic strength, individual species concentrations, or solid-phase composition.\n\n### Relation to the supplied local archival relationship\n\nThe supplied archival relationship concerned a much lower amount (0.001 mol) and a volume change from 0.018 to 0.054 L, predicting an increase of 0.005806 in acid-dissociation fraction and 0.002560 in pH_normalized. My experiment did not include that amount or those volumes. It therefore does **not** directly validate or falsify that local claim.\n\nIn my higher-loading range, the pH direction on dilution was positive and hence qualitatively compatible with the archival pH direction. In contrast, mean dissociation fraction decreased slightly upon dilution at both tested amounts, rather than increasing. Because the effects are small and the regimes do not overlap, the proper conclusion is that the archival relationship is not established as transferable to this region; it should remain a local prior rather than be promoted to a general law.\n\n### Coupling interpretation\n\nThe results are consistent with a coupled system in which nominal reagent loading alters both acid-base speciation and the quality or conditioning of the equilibrium proxy. The near-constant precipitation signal argues against precipitation being the only control variable, but does not exclude a subdominant role. A plausible interaction is:\n\n1. nominal loading changes effective concentration and nonideality;\n2. nonideality shifts an effective acid-dissociation response;\n3. a weak precipitation or association channel changes the free-species pool without producing a large movement in the normalized precipitation proxy;\n4. pH responds only weakly because buffering, activity effects, or hidden charge-balancing species moderate the free hydrogen response.\n\nThis is a useful effective explanation, not a uniquely identified microscopic mechanism.\n\n### What remains unidentified\n\nThe following quantities cannot be inferred from the public observations:\n\n- a thermodynamic pKa or equilibrium constant;\n- the identities and concentrations of the acid, conjugate base, counterions, buffers, complexes, or precipitated phase;\n- whether the precipitation signal is proportional to solid amount, supersaturation, particle abundance, or another synthetic proxy;\n- ionic strength, activity coefficients, phase partitioning, and mass balance among unobserved species;\n- temperature dependence, time-to-equilibrium, hysteresis, and the effects of catalysts or non-water solvents;\n- whether the observed loading response is driven by reagent concentration itself, by total solute concentration, or by a hidden formulation component.\n\nThe design also confounds concentration with total amount only partially: both amount and volume were varied factorially, but only at two levels each. It can detect broad directional effects, not curvature, thresholds, or a fully parameterized interaction surface.\n\n### Reasonable competing explanations\n\n1. **Concentration-dependent weak-acid nonideality.** The observed lower dissociation fraction at higher amount and weak pH changes on dilution could arise from activity coefficients or association shifting an effective pKa. This is the leading effective explanation.\n\n2. **Buffering by an unobserved acid/base inventory.** A hidden buffer could hold pH near 4.1 while allowing the reported dissociation fraction to move independently. This explains the narrow pH range and is observationally difficult to distinguish from nonideality using the present channels.\n\n3. **Coupled precipitation or ion pairing.** A portion of the conjugate base or another species may be removed into an unobserved associated/condensed state. The public precipitation proxy is nonzero, but its weak variation means this explanation cannot be confirmed or assigned a stoichiometry.\n\n4. **Proxy-specific response rather than literal bulk speciation.** The final-assay outputs are public synthetic processed estimates. A shared latent state could generate pH, dissociation, and precipitation channels without each being a direct species measurement. This is especially important when interpreting an apparent pKa.\n\nThese explanations are empirically equivalent over much of the present matrix. The current evidence supports an effective loading- and dilution-sensitive equilibrium description, but not selection of one microscopic explanation.\n\n### Scope and confidence statement\n\nThe supported scope is this bounded synthetic, water-only equilibrium benchmark at 0.010\u20130.030 mol nominal reagent and 0.040\u20130.080 L liquid volume, after the specified terminal closeout. Within that range, I am confident in the qualitative findings of mildly acidic pH, low nonzero acid-dissociation fraction, no large precipitation transition, and a strong loading dependence of the environment diagnostic. I have moderate confidence that loading suppresses the observed dissociation fraction and that dilution slightly increases pH. I have low confidence in the sign or magnitude of dilution\u2019s effect on acid dissociation and in any inferred microscopic or thermodynamic interpretation.\n\nOutside this tested range\u2014including the archival low-loading anchor, other solvents, catalysts, altered temperature, or substantially different volumes\u2014the equations above are extrapolations only. They should be treated as testable hypotheses rather than established laws."
}

That is a possible inconsistency with K1\u2019s stated scope limitation.\n\nQ11 and Q12 were more reliable. Q11 was close to Batch 9, and Q12 lay inside the observed concentration range near Batches 4-6. Q01 and Q02 were near but slightly below the Batch 2 dilute anchor, so they were moderate extrapolations rather than severe ones.\n\n7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation and how to test it\n\nThe sealed recommendation selected Batch 1 as the final evidentiary anchor, not as an optimized or proven-best condition. Batch 1 was chosen because it matched the archival local anchor, 0.001 mol in 0.018 L water, and therefore was the clearest reference for checking the supplied dilution relationship. Its score, about 0.2555, was not the sample-best score; Batch 7 had a higher observed score around 0.3207.\n\nTherefore the recommendation has several limitations. It is not proof of optimality, not proof of reproducibility, and not proof of broad robustness. It is a sample-internal reference selection. It also depends on the decision that mechanistic anchoring was more important than score.\n\nTo test repeatability, I would run exact replicates of Batch 1 across multiple independent vessel starts and compare pH_normalized, alpha, precipitation, residual, and score. To test local robustness, I would perturb Batch 1 around 0.001 mol and 0.018 L, for example small changes in volume and loading, and check whether the archival dilution trend holds locally. To test cross-material scope, I would repeat the anchor and dilution pair in ethanol, acetonitrile, and toluene if legal and meaningful under the task\u2019s solvent system. To test cross-world generality, the same design would need to be repeated in independent ChemWorld episodes or cards, because the present campaign is a bounded synthetic world.\n\nThe key distinction is: Batch 1 is an interpretable sample-internal anchor. It is not the highest-scoring sample and not a demonstrated optimum. Batch 7 is the sample-internal highest score among my 12, but even Batch 7 is only sample-best, not proven optimal, because the design did not search the full continuous action space and included no local optimization or replicate confirmation."
